title: USS Lincoln sails past Singapore after 9-month deployment
summary: Associated Press journalists on the Indonesian island of Batam, across the Singapore Strait, spotted the massive vessel as it transited waters near Singapore just after 1 a.m. local time.
story: The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln sailed past Singapore early on Sunday as it headed home after a grueling deployment in the Middle East. It's expected to stop in Thailand for a port visit.
Associated Press journalists on the Indonesian island of Batam, across the Singapore Strait, spotted the massive vessel as it transited waters near Singapore just after 1 a.m. local time.
The Japan-based USS George Washington, another U.S. aircraft carrier, arrived earlier this month in the Middle East to replace the USS Lincoln.

The Lincoln, one of the U.S. Navy's largest warships, was supporting the U.S. war against Iran. Its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days. Concerns have grown about the Lincoln's lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products.
Thai officials have said the Lincoln will stop in Thailand for rest and recovery before returning to its U.S. base.

The USS Abraham Lincoln and its roughly 5,000 crew members left San Diego on Nov. 21. The war with Iran, which began in February, extended the mission and intensified their workload. The ship has served as a launch point for thousands of aircraft flights supporting the strikes.

Family members have voiced concerns about deteriorating sanitary and mental health conditions, and alleged food shortages. U.S. Central Command said reports of increased suicidal ideation among the crew were false, and said there have been no deaths aboard the vessel. The circumstances of an incident on Aug. 3 where a sailor fell overboard and was recovered remain under investigation, according to a Navy statement. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said at the time that  reports of issues onboard the aircraft carried had been "misrepresented."

Jefferson Kelley, whose son Jackson is aboard the Lincoln on his first-ever deployment, told "CBS Mornings" earlier this month that he would "get on a plane or helicopter tonight to get shipped out to the Lincoln if it meant bringing him home to his mom and his siblings and his family."
"They should not be deployed this long," Kelley said. "These are old ships. It's not like they're even state-of-the-art. And they take a lot of maintenance, a lot of work. It's around the clock."

title: Iceland rejects EU membership talks in referendum vote
summary: The country is already part of the European Economic Area and the Schengen Area, which allows frictionless movement of people, goods, capital and services.
story: Icelanders have rejected plans to resume negotiations to join the European Union more than a decade after previous talks stalled, the national broadcaster reported Sunday.

In a vote held Saturday, 52.8 percent of Icelanders rejected the resumption of EU entry talks suspended 13 years ago, while 47.2 percent voted 'Yes', according to the official tally published by RUV, the public broadcaster.
"The nation rejects accession negotiations with the EU," RUV wrote.

The small North Atlantic island is already a close ally of the EU, as a member of the European Economic Area and the Schengen zone, which in practical terms allows easier movement of people, capital, goods and services. Norway and Liechtenstein are the only other European countries which share the same relationship with the EU.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
The vote will put the long-debated issue to rest for the second time. A euroskeptic government ended EU talks in 2015.

Iceland's left-leaning coalition government, elected in 2024, moved up the EU referendum it had planned for next year after President Trump mistakenly named the country four times  while speaking about his designs on Greenland.
It was a simple yes-or-no question for roughly 265,000 eligible voters: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?

Opponents rallied around fishing and the fact that Iceland already reaps benefits from being in the EU's frictionless single market and the Schengen free-travel zone without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They argued that Iceland's voice would be muted in the large European Parliament and that it would be better off cutting its own trade deals, such as one with China.

Backers said EU membership would lower inflation and interest rates, and the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna. They said it was also in the nation's interest to get closer to its European neighbors to tackle issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change.

title: Trump says U.S. now has control of over 60 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves
summary: President Trump announced a deal to grant the U.S. control of more than 60 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves.
story: President Trump announced a deal Friday to grant the United States majority control of over 60 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves — as the Trump administration angles to get oil companies to return to the country after a U.S. military operation replaced the country's leadership earlier this year.
Mr. Trump said in a social media post the deal was made "at no cost to the American Taxpayer" and was struck "through a partnership with private business."

A U.S. official told CBS News that interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez granted a private joint venture a 100-year concession to operate in oil fields that make up 65 billion barrels of petroleum. The venture is a "joint project of the U.S. government and an experienced private operator in Venezuela."
The U.S. government will control 55% of the joint venture, split between equity in the venture and the ability to obtain oil from it at cost, the official said.

The official described the venture as the world's second-largest corporate owner of proven oil reserves, after Saudi Aramco. It's not clear which private companies will be involved in the venture, but only a handful of foreign oil and gas companies have maintained a presence in Venezuela, including U.S.-based Chevron, Spain-based Repsol and Italy-based Eni.

"This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity," the president wrote on Truth Social.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on social media the deal will "bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs, and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy."

Rodriguez confirmed the deal in a statement on X, calling it a "historic agreement" that will "have a significant impact on our nation's revival." She estimated that it will generate over $209 billion in tax revenue for the Venezuelan government.

The deal marks the Trump administration's latest effort to lure oil investment to the South American country, as it seeks to push down oil prices — though expanding production in Venezuela could be a longer-term endeavor.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, at just over 300 billion barrels, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. By comparison, the U.S. has less than 50 billion barrels.

But the country's oil industry has long struggled with underinvestment, decrepit infrastructure and tight sanctions. And many major oil companies — like ConocoPhillips and ExxonMobil — left Venezuela when former President Hugo Chávez nationalized their assets almost two decades ago, leaving them wary of doing business in the country. Chevron was the only major U.S. company to maintain its presence in Venezuela.

In January, U.S. military forces captured Chávez's successor, Nicolás Maduro, causing former Vice President Rodriguez to assume power. Rodriguez and the Trump administration have sought to cooperate, including on energy.

Since then, Mr. Trump has encouraged American companies to reenter Venezuela, meeting with executives of major oil and gas firms to pitch them on the country's vast oil reserves. The U.S. Treasury Department has eased sanctions on Venezuela's oil industry, and Rodriguez signed legislation that allows private companies to manage oil extraction.
Some firms have expressed interest, with the independent Hunt Oil Company reportedly inking a deal earlier this month with the state-run Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A.

Others have expressed some hesitation, pointing to the fraught history of Venezuela's oil industry. During a White House event earlier this year, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said "there's an opportunity in Venezuela," but he called the country "uninvestable" until changes are made to the country's legal and economic system. He noted that ExxonMobil's assets in Venezuela were subjected to two different waves of nationalization in the 1970s and 2000s.

"We've had our assets seized there twice," Woods said in January, before Venezuela passed its oil industry reforms. "To reenter a third time would require some pretty significant changes from what we've historically seen here and what is currently the state."

title: Ontario premier slams Trump's order: "It's Lake Ontario now and forever"
summary: Amid an ongoing trade war​ between Canada and the United States, President Trump last week sought to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" by executive order.
story: Ontario's head of government on Saturday erected a sign by Lake Ontario that reads "Lake Ontario - Now and Always" and criticized President Trump after he signed an executive order to rename the body of water that connects the Canadian province and the state of New York.
"I'm here on the shores of beautiful Lake Ontario, a crown jewel of our province and our country," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in a short video message posted on social media.

"You may have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake, all because he doesn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves," he said. "But let's be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario, and long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario."
Ford added that the province put the huge blue sign to remind Mr. Trump and everyone that "it's Lake Ontario now and forever."
The new sign, which also says in French "Lac Ontario - Aujourd'hui et pour toujours," is located at Fifty Point Conservation Area, a park in Hamilton, Ontario.

Amid an ongoing trade war between Canada and the United States, Mr. Trump last week sought to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" by an executive order. He also said the U.S. doesn't expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer."
The name Ontario came from the Iroquoian word "oniatarí:io," and means "lake of shining waters," according to the Center for Great Lakes Literacy.

The leader of the Seneca Nation, one of the Iroquoian-speaking nations in the region, on Friday also criticized Mr. Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario and called for the executive order to be rescinded.

Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca said the order violates a more than 225-year-old treaty and shows a "blatant disrespect" for the Indigenous people who gave it its name in the first place. He said the Lake Ontario name should remain as a reflection of the Indigenous people in the U.S. and Canada who lived in territory around and along the lake long before the creation of either nation.
"The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action," he said in a statement.

Following failed trade talks between the two nations, the U.S. began imposing 50% tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods. Mr. Trump also announced that the U.S. will impose a 50% tariff on all Canadian automotive and steel imports beginning in January, while claiming that "Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney then announced new retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., saying that it would impose tariffs of up to 50% on about $20 billion of U.S. imports.
In recent days, Ford has openly pushed back against Mr. Trump's treatment of Canada.

"He's treating us like we're Communist China here," Ford told CBS News chief Washington correspondent Major Garrett last week. "We're the closest friends and allies that the U.S. has anywhere in the entire world, and I want to keep it that way."

Ford and Mr. Trump traded harsh words as the trade war escalates. The president called Ford "unimpressive" and a "flunky" of Carney, who belongs to a different political party but has drawn support from the Ontario premier.
Ford, for his part, has called the U.S. president a "dictator" and said: "I have a lot of real estate on my a**, so he has a lot of room to kiss my a**."

title: Trump-shaped ecstasy pills are potentially lethal, Dutch institute says
summary: Ecstasy pills shaped to look like President Trump contain a high concentration of the chemical PMMA, which could potentially be lethal, a Dutch institute said.
story: A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute warned users on Friday about potentially lethal ecstasy pills shaped to look like the head of President Trump.
The respected Trimbos Institute said that several of the pills have been handed in recently at a network of centers that test drugs for users before they take them.

The institute warned in a "Red Alert" published on its website and social media that they contain a high concentration of a chemical called PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine. The chemical is similar to MDMA, the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.

The institute says if PMMA is found in an ecstasy pill, then the pill is contaminated and could be lethal. Users don't feel the effect of the drug right away, the institute said, and could take a higher dosage, which could lead to overheating, epileptic seizures, loss of consciousness or heart problems.
"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute warned.

It released a photo of the pills that have a depiction of Mr. Trump's head on one side and on the other side "NL" and "Trump" stamped into the surface on either side of a vertical line. One of the pills has a green face, and another is yellow.
"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she told The Associated Press.

Producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, but it's widely used, particularly at clubs and music festivals. A government report in 2024 said that some 550,000 people took the drug in a year.
The Trimbos Institute tests drugs through its national network of 12 participants and 34 testing locations in the Netherlands.

title: ICE deports Venezuelan father from Texas to West Africa
summary: Carlos Tellez Sanchez had worked at a car dealership in Dallas during the day and drove for Uber Eats at night to support his family.
story: A 35-year-old Venezuelan man who lived in Texas for years is now nearly 6,000 miles from his wife and 5-month-old American son after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported him to West Africa.

Carlos Tellez Sanchez said he had never heard of Liberia until last week, when he found out he was being deported to the country that sits between Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire just hours before his flight took off. He said he spent the 15-hour flight across the Atlantic in handcuffs, and is now stranded in a remote area of the West African nation.
"I do not understand how a country that considers itself a global hero can act this way towards a human being," he told CBS News in Spanish over a video call.

Tellez Sanchez said he now spends much of his time inside a hotel more than an hour away from Monrovia, Liberia's capital, where he was placed alongside deportees from Brazil, Colombia, Honduras and other countries.

President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration has intensified this summer, with ICE making a record number of arrests. Increasingly, some detainees are being sent to countries that are not their own and banished to far-flung places. Tellez Sanchez, who entered the U.S. illegally five years ago, is one of them.

The Venezuela native had been in the U.S. since 2021 after fleeing his home country. He worked at a car dealership in Dallas during the day and drove for Uber Eats at night to support his family. CBS News could not find any criminal charges or convictions for Tellez Sanchez, beyond civil immigration violations.

In December 2025, Tellez Sanchez was detained by ICE during what he expected would be a routine immigration appointment. He spent eight months in ICE detention centers before his deportation to Africa.

An immigration judge in 2021 granted Tellez Sanchez protection from being sent back to Venezuela, finding that he could be persecuted there. Legally, however, that order did not prevent ICE from deporting him to any other country.

Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration has brokered so-called "third country" deportation agreements with dozens of nations around the world, including some notoriously dangerous places like South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

Tellez Sanchez' brother in Dallas, Juan Tellez, said he has no idea why Tellez Sanchez was sent to Liberia and that no one has given him an explanation. He described his brother as a good person and a hard worker who "doesn't deserve what happened to him."

In a statement to CBS News late Friday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tellez Sanchez had been deported from the U.S. once before crossing the southern border illegally in 2021. DHS said he was then released under the Biden administration until his arrest by ICE during a check-in appointment on Dec. 19.

DHS said Tellez Sanchez refused "several opportunities to be removed to Mexico," adding that he was "removed to a safe third country on August 19," presumably Liberia. DHS did not dispute that Tellez Sanchez lacks a criminal record.

"If an illegal alien chooses to file a claim in court refusing to go to their home country, we are required by law to find a safe and secure nation for them to go to," DHS added in its statement. "If an illegal alien chooses to go home, we will give them a free flight home and a $3,000 check. The choice is theirs."
In Liberia, Tellez Sanchez says he has no clear plan.
"It's a very difficult situation," he said, "one that I don't wish on anybody."

title: U.S. takes out refueling station for alleged drug-trafficking boats
summary: The vessel, which was in international waters near Ecuador, was allegedly used as a floating refueling station for drug boats belonging to the Los Choneros organization.
story: The U.S. military, in conjunction with Ecuadorian officials, boarded and later sank a vessel on Friday allegedly used as a refueling station for drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean, according to U.S. Southern Command.
The vessel, which was in international waters near Ecuador, was allegedly used as a floating ship-to-ship refueling station for drug boats belonging to the Los Choneros organization.

The ship was boarded by Marines and sailors from the USS San Antonio and cleared without incident, SOCOM said. The people taken off the boat were then taken to Ecuador, and the U.S. sank the boat with an airstrike, SOCOM said, which also provided video of the ship being scuttled.

"Today's operation is a stark example of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition's power to dismantle the sophisticated, clandestine narco-terrorist tactics and capabilities that have enabled the trafficking of dangerous drugs destined for American communities," SOCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said in a statement. "Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region. Together with our regional partners, we are committed to defeating narco-terrorists in the Western Hemisphere."

"Today's interdiction and sinking of a floating refueling station used for at-sea drug trafficking operations dealt a direct blow to the logistics network fueling narco-terrorists and cartels in the Western Hemisphere.By severing this critical maritime node, our Joint Force —… pic.twitter.com/lg7aesU5vH

The strike comes as the U.S. continues to target alleged drug traffickers with deadly strikes on small boats in the eastern Pacific and Caribbean. The latest strike came on Tuesday when four people were killed in a boat strike in the Caribbean.

That attack brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" almost a year ago.

The last strike on an alleged drug boat in the Pacific Ocean came on Sunday, when two people were killed. It was the first strike after a pause of more than two months in the U.S. campaign against alleged smugglers.

Ecuadorian officials have been battling the Los Choneros gang for years. The drug-trafficking organization, named for the city of Chone in western Ecuador, was led for years by José Adolfo Macías Villamar.

Macías escaped from jail in 2024 while serving a 34-year sentence for drug trafficking, after which a large-scale gang war broke out on the streets of the capital of Quito. The gang wars expanded to Guayaquil and the nearby town of Nobol. Gunmen even stormed a studio in Guayaquil and fired off shots on live TV. New President Daniel Noboa was forced to call in the army to quell the violence.

Macías, who was indicted by the U.S. Department of Justice on drug and weapons charges in April 2025, was recaptured two months later and extradited to the U.S. in July 2025. He pleaded not guilty to charges that he imported thousands of pounds of cocaine into the United States. He is still awaiting trial.

title: Russian strike on Ukrainian warehouse kills 37, one of deadliest attacks of 2026
summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy suggested warehouse near a residential area hit by a Russian strike was used to store ammunition.
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday the country's authorities had opened an investigation and were looking into possible official "negligence" after a Russian drone strike on a warehouse near Kyiv triggered a large detonation and killed at least 37 people.
"There are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said in a social media post on Saturday morning.
The president did not explicitly say what had caused the detonation or what the warehouse was storing when it was attacked.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions," Zelenskyy said.

The attack sparked a fire in the Bucha district, west of Kyiv, that swept through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the local regional military administration.
Among the dead, Zelenskyy said, was the head of the Dmytrivka community, Taras Didych, who had been working to rescue people.
"Appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn," Zelenskyy added.

In a statement, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said that it had attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics center and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.

Zelenskyy later announced that two officials from state-owned companies, including Ukraine's largest arms producer, Ukroboronprom, had illegally allowed the storage of weapons on the site in Vyshneve and would be held accountable.
The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general said a drone "fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla."
"A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise's grounds, and detonation began," it added.

The prosecutor's office specified that its investigation would focus on "the legality of the... storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise's grounds", as well as whether the company, which was not named, had the "necessary permits and approvals."
Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned after a previous deadly attack in July in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, on a munitions depot.
That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of the state-owned company, which did not comply with standards despite the proximity of residential buildings.

title: Couple recounts surviving deadly Nepal flood: "I knew I was going to die"
summary: A California couple were in a Nepali village when an avalanche of powerful waters ripped down from the high Himalayas toward them.
story: A couple from the San Francisco Bay Area who were on a pilgrimage to Tibet told CBS News on Friday that they thought they were going to die when they saw a mountain of water coming toward them earlier this week.
"I knew I was going to die," Anjana Raja told CBS News. "I knew I was going to die."

The catastrophic flash flooding that struck a mountainous border area of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday — when a glacier in the Himalayas collapsed and sent torrents of water into the valleys below — has killed nearly 600 people, with an estimated 2,500 more believed to be missing as search and rescue crews frantically scour for survivors.
The U.S. State Department said Friday that about 90 Americans are estimated to be among the missing.

When the avalanche of powerful waters ripped down from the high Himalayas, the melting glacier and debris first hit the Nepali village of Timure, near where Raja and her partner Pattabiraman Venkatesan were with their tour bus.

The couple were making their first pilgrimage to Tibet, an autonomous region of China that shares a border with Nepal. They had driven through Timure, and were in the bus in Nepal's Rasuwa District, near the Nepal-China border, when what looked like a tsunami appeared.

"It's like 60, 70 feet, it looked like a tsunami, but dark black," Venkatesan   said. "... I could see this monster thing coming down. At that point I didn't know if it was water. I thought it was fire, forest fire, honestly."
Raja said she grabbed Venkatesan   by the collar, pulled him and said, "Run," as the two of them jumped off the bus.
As thousands of people ran for their lives, cellphone videos showed some getting swallowed into the churn, while others were able to climb to safety higher up and were eventually airlifted out.
The couple said they sprinted up a set of steps trying to reach higher ground.
"Along the way, you know, houses were coming down, it was bringing down homes," Venkatesan said.
Raja said she could hear the screams of people who were being swept away by the floodwaters below.
"I saw death right in front of my eyes," Raja said.
A guide led them up to a flat area at the top of a nearby mountain. The climb was treacherous.
"So tall up, I don't know even how we climbed," Raja said. "It was really hard."
Venkatesan described the climb as "narrow and so slippery," with "mud and stones and rocks and everything."
They spent that night in a goat shed with several other survivors, including local residents and tourists, and were airlifted out the following day.
The couple said everyone aboard their tour bus survived.
"The fact that we survived is nothing short of a miracle," Venkatesan said.
The couple are counting their blessings. Venkatesan   said the experience has given them a renewed appreciation for life.
"It strengthens my thought on life," Venkatesan   said. "Be good, do good, think good, and leave the rest to whoever is above us. That's all I can say."

title: Nepal flood rescue efforts intensify as number of missing soars past 2,000
summary: Rescuers pulled out survivors and helicopters ferried people to safety as Nepal and China raced to respond after catastrophic flash floods​ killed hundreds of people.
story: Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety Friday as Nepal and China raced to respond after catastrophic flash floods and landslides killed almost 600 people and left roughly 2,500 missing.

Nepali and Chinese authorities warned of further risk of flooding from a new lake that has formed upstream following Wednesday's disaster, telling people in the potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far, but 1,924 people remain unaccounted for in the country, according to authorities. China's state media previously said 558 people were missing on the Chinese side.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said Friday that the confirmed death toll had risen to 579. Local Nepalese media said there could still be as many as 12,000 people unaccounted for, but that much higher figure was not confirmed by any officials. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners who were in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak on the Tibet side of the border.

Helicopters had carried more than 3,000 people to safety in Kathmandu and other locations. On the Chinese side, there was little information about survivors, although the death toll rose to five Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders' efforts to direct relief efforts.

The Red Cross said Friday that some 90,000 people had likely been impacted by the flooding, which is believed to have been triggered by the collapse of a rocky ledge and the vast portion of a glacier it had supported.

The Nepal Police issued a fresh alert Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibetan side of the border was running over. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and immediately move to a safe location if necessary.

It was unclear if that concern was related to fears of flooding from an overflowing barrier lake that formed behind a dam formed by debris from the initial flash floods, high up on the Chinese side of the Himalayan mountains.
Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said the rescue operation "hasn't stopped," but was continuing under high alert.

Although Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Friday that the lake was more than 6 miles from Gyirong Port, the border crossing with Nepal that was decimated by a wall of mud and water on Wednesday morning, it said the risk of flooding was high. It said the lake was at an elevation of 9,680 feet, about 3,280 feet above Gyirong Port.
CCTV later said flood risks from the overflowing lake were deemed "manageable," Reuters reported.
Nepali army rescuers were working to help people trapped in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.
In video from the scene, rescuers half-pulled, half-pushed a man covered in dark brown mud out of the tunnel. He was one of dozens who were likely trapped inside.
Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press the focus was on survivors.
"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."
What caused the flash floods?

Scientists said satellite images indicated that bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The rocks and melted water suddenly swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing torrents of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Scientists were still piecing together information from satellite and ground-level data to confirm exactly what caused the flood, but Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria who is currently based in Bangladesh, said "a lower part of a glacier has really come off," noting satellite images that he said made it look "like someone cut with a huge knife through the whole lower part" of the rock and ice.
The Hindu Kush Himalayan region is warming rapidly, driving major changes in glaciers, snow cover, permafrost and mountain slopes, according to climate scientists.
Around 78% of the glacier area, located between about 14,760 and 19,685 feet above sea level, is highly exposed to warming.
"What happened yesterday is unfortunately the new normal. It's going to get worse from here onwards," Steiner said.
Americans among the missing
U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said Friday morning on Fox News that 90 Americans were among those still missing in the wake of the disaster, with five having been rescued.

In a statement, the U.S. Embassy in Nepal said the U.S. was "delivering a range of supplies requested by the Government of Nepal and is working with Nepal to ensure that assistance reaches the people who need it."

"Catholic Relief Services, working through implementing partner Caritas Nepal, will deliver more than 2.5 metric tons of food supplies, 500 blankets, 500 mosquito nets, and 500 insulating foam sheets for temporary shelter flooring to two school locations in Rasuwa," the embassy said, noting plans for subsequent supply shipments were already in place.
President Trump called the flooding terrible to see on Thursday, saying that "strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks."
He told reporters in the Oval Office that U.S. officials had spoken with Nepalese leaders and offered to provide "anything they want."

Leslie Crespi, a community liaison for the Isha Foundation, a volunteer-run group that promotes well-being founded by Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru Vasudev, told CBS News about 80 people who were taking part in a pilgrimage run by the group in the region were missing.

"At this point we are awaiting word," Crespi said in a phone interview from McMinnville, Tennessee, of the missing pilgrims. "We have done as much outreach as we can through the State Department, through the embassy."

The 80 people are from 19 countries, Crespi said, including 22 from the U.S. Crespi said about 1,000 people in total were taking part in the pilgrimage. The 22 missing Americans were all adults, and included 13 women and nine men, the foundation later said in data it provided to CBS News.
She said the Isha Foundation has organized pilgrimages for 21 years, and "in those 21 years, we have never lost a life."

U.S. citizen Deepak Dandu said his wife, Sridevi Vejella, was among those missing in Nepal. She was on the pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation to Mount Kailash in Tibet — a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others — which he said was a "lifelong dream" for her.
He told CBS News she was crossing from China into Nepal when the flood hit. The foundation told him she was part of a group that was present at the Gyirong Port immigration complex.
Dandu was getting ready to board a flight to Hyderabad, India, to join his son.
"He is going through a lot, hearing all the news," Dandu said of his son. "I think he is really upset. I'm trying to go there and be with him."
"10 or so seconds saved some of us"

Videos of Wednesday's disaster showed floodwaters destroying buildings, bridges and vehicles as people ran in front of the stories-high torrent. In the aftermath, broken concrete lay upended in expanses of brown mud that also caked buildings and buried streets.

Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China. Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. Wednesday and was busy working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

"Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us," he recalled from Kathmandu, where he was back with family. "We all immediately started running out and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us."

Gaire said he didn't remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but his 15 colleagues were missing. "It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don't call it a flood, it was a tsunami."
He described Timure as a vibrant place filled with government offices, hotels, cafes, banks, primary schools, tea shops and residential buildings, where more than 1,500 people were living.

Anjana Raja and Pattabiraman Venkatesan, a couple from the San Francisco Bay Area who were on a pilgrimage to Tibet, told CBS News in an interview Friday that they had just passed Timure headed to the border when what looked like a tsunami struck Wednesday while they were in their tour bus.

"It's like 60, 70 feet, it looked like a tsunami, but dark black," Venkatesan said. "... I could see this monster thing coming down. At that point I didn't know if it was water. I thought it was fire, forest fire, honestly."
The couple made it out of the bus and ran for higher ground.
"Along the way, you know, houses were coming down, it was bringing down homes," Venkatesan said.
"I knew I was going to die," Anjana Raja said. "I knew I was going to die."
They eventually climbed their way to a mountaintop, where they spent the night in a goat shed with other survivors, and were airlifted out the following day.
"The fact that we survived is nothing short of a miracle," Venkatesan said.

title: Tigers, jaguars, bison found in raid on fuel smugglers near U.S. border
summary: Smuggling gasoline and diesel from the U.S. into Mexico and reselling it tax-free is a huge money-maker for organized crime gangs, including drug cartels.
story: Mexican authorities said Thursday that they had rescued Bengal tigers, mandrills, hyenas and even a camel during raids on a fuel smuggling ring in the northeastern state of Tamaulipas, on the U.S. border.
The 135 animals found at a ranch also included lions, buffalo, sulcata tortoises, spider monkeys, jaguars, an American bison and a green macaw.
Thirty-five of the animals, including the green macaw and sulcata tortoise, are classified as endangered species.

Mexican authorities regularly rescue exotic animals from properties owned by wealthy drug traffickers. Some Mexican drug cartels are known to house exotic cats as symbols of power and, occasionally, to dispose of their enemies.  According to a 2023 U.S. indictment, some victims of a Sinaloa cartel faction were "fed dead or alive to tigers."
On this occasion, however, the military found them during an operation targeting fuel smugglers.
Smuggling gasoline and diesel from the United States into Mexico and reselling it tax-free is a huge money-maker for organized crime gangs, including drug cartels.
During these latest raids on five properties, the military seized 18,000 gallons of diesel, fuel tanks, pumps, firearms, and tools.
One person was arrested.
Mexican authorities cracked down on fuel smuggling in 2025, when high-ranking navy officers and officials were implicated in the illegal trade.
Some 10 billion liters of black market fuel were seized at that time in Tamaulipas.
The attorney general's office on Thursday formally charged Fernando Farias, a high-ranking officer who was expelled last week from Argentina, with fuel smuggling.
A former governor of Tamaulipas, Ernesto Ruffo, was also recently arrested on charges of fuel theft.
Fuel smuggling a growing problem
Fuel theft — more commonly known as huachicol in Mexico — has risen to the second most profitable revenue stream for Mexican cartels behind drug trafficking, according to the U.S. Treasury.
U.S. officials allege that some cartel members steal fuel and crude oil from Pemex by bribing insiders, tapping pipelines, siphoning refineries, hijacking tanker trucks, and intimidating employees.

The stolen fuel is then sold across Mexico, the United States and Central America, while crude oil is smuggled north via complicit brokers — frequently disguised as "waste oil" to evade taxes and environmental scrutiny, the U.S. Treasury discovered.

Once inside the United States, the oil is then funneled to unscrupulous importers along the southwest border, sold at deep discounts on U.S. and global markets with proceeds quietly funneled back to the cartels.
U.S. authorities have even accused the Jalisco New Generation cartel of operating its own service stations.

The United States has been cracking down. In June, the U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on two Mexican men and nine companies involved in transportation, financial services and real estate, accused of being tied to a cartel-linked fuel theft ring.
In December, the Treasury Department imposed sanctions on a violent Mexican fuel-theft cartel and its imprisoned leader, nicknamed "The Sledgehammer."

title: 2 airport workers die of malaria from mosquito on plane in Germany
summary: Caused by parasites spread via Anopheles mosquitoes, malaria can cause symptoms including nausea, headache and intense waves of fever and chills.
story: Two workers at Germany's Frankfurt airport who caught malaria from a mosquito thought to have arrived on a plane have died, the city's health authority said this week.
Airport officials had earlier said one employee had perished, with six workers infected.
The Robert Koch Institute said an imported Anopheles mosquito carried over by an aircraft was the likely cause.
The other four infected employees were hospitalized and receiving treatment, said an airport spokesman.
Traps have been installed at the airport and mosquitoes captured will be analyzed in a laboratory to determine their species and origin, BBC News reported.
"We have provided comprehensive information to all employees and encourage them to consult a doctor if they experience any symptoms," an airport spokesperson told the BBC.
According to the RKI, Germany's last outbreak of airport-based malaria was in 2023. The rarity of the condition means diagnosis can be delayed, increasing the chances of severe symptoms.

The institute said malaria in Germany almost exclusively affects long-haul travelers who were infected in malaria-endemic areas, and that malaria transmitted within a German airport is rare, the BBC reported.

"For the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low. The disease is not transmissible from person to person but is always transmitted by mosquitoes," public health officials in Frankfurt said in a letter obtained by the BBC.
Officials said laboratory tests to determine the source of the infections were not expected to be available for several weeks.
The Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, Belgium, said it would analyze the malaria parasites in the patients' blood samples.
Caused by parasites spread via Anopheles mosquitoes, malaria can cause symptoms including nausea, headache and intense waves of fever and chills.
The disease causes hundreds of thousands of deaths a year, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.
Treatments exist and patients caught early with the disease usually make a complete recovery.

title: Jimi Hendrix’s final words to roadie revealed after violent Hells Angels clash
summary: Eric Barrett recalls Jimi Hendrix's final concert at the Isle of Fehmarn, where Hells Angels violence forced a harrowing escape before his death.
story: Carlos Santana recalls the moment he impressed Jimi Hendrix
It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend's final official concert performance.

Eric Barrett, who was Hendrix's roadie and confidant from 1968 to 1970, has written a memoir, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." Barrett went on to spend nearly five decades working behind the scenes with other iconic artists, including Madonna, David Bowie and Aerosmith.

"We were playing on the Isle of Fehmarn, and the Hells Angels had taken over," Barrett recalled to Fox News Digital. "There was no control. It was a scary place to be. We had two cars there waiting to get us off the island and go back to London. But the Hells Angels didn't want us to get off the island. They wanted the boys to stay and party. And then it got violent."
PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK
Jimi Hendrix is the subject of a new book by his roadie and tour manager, Eric Barrett, titled, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." (David Redfern/Redferns)

According to Barrett's book, hundreds of Hells Angels descended on the island and took over the venue. He wrote that many fans who had been camping out were "beaten and robbed" as festival security was chased off. Hendrix, he said, took one look at the mayhem and retreated to his room "alone, sober." The outlaw motorcycle club had taken over.

The next day, Hendrix took the stage and was met with boos. He told the hostile audience, "I don't give a f--- if you boo, as long as you boo in key, you mothers," before chuckling. When he was done, Hendrix told the audience, "Thank you, goodbye. Peace!"
"Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond" by Eric Barrett is out now. (Diversion Books)
Barrett ushered Hendrix and the band off the stage toward the waiting cars. Barrett was eager to get out. But then the bikers surrounded them.
WATCH: CARLOS SANTANA RECALLS THE MOMENT HE IMPRESSED JIMI HENDRIX: ‘I’LL TAKE IT’

"I saw a Hells Angel about to hit [tour manager] Gerry Stickells over the head with this baton," said Barrett. "I put my arm up to take the blow. I nearly passed out from the pain, but imagine if it had landed on Gerry's skull? We managed to get inside the car. Jimi kept looking at me because he saw me take the blow. He just said to me, 'Are you OK, Eric? Are you OK?' He kept asking me if I was OK. That's just the kind of man he was. And... that was the last thing he ever said to me."
Eric Barrett was Jimi Hendrix's roadie from 1968 to 1970. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)
On Sept. 18, 1970, paramedics arrived at Monika Dannemann's apartment at the Samarkand Hotel in London and found Hendrix unresponsive. He was 27.
Stickells broke the news to Barrett.
An exterior view of the former Samarkand Hotel in London, where Jimi Hendrix died in 1970. (Future Publishing via Getty Images)

"I couldn't believe it," said Barrett. "I remember walking around London in a fog. It was a stupid, tragic accident. He took too many of [girlfriend] Monika Dannemann's sleeping pills. She supposedly had these incredibly powerful German tranquilizers. And she said he took nine of them. She couldn't wake him. She called Eric Burdon of The Animals, who was a good friend of Jimi's. He screamed at her, 'Call the f-----g ambulance!'"
From left: Friends Jimi Hendrix, Eric Burdon and Noel Redding. (Sygma via Getty Images)
"What I'm being told was the ambulance guys ... laid him on his back, and he threw up," said Barrett. "He asphyxiated. That was the accident. The pills were the accident. Tragedy was him dying."
Jimi Hendrix performs at the Isle of Wight festival on August 29, 1970. (Jean-Pierre Leloir)

In the book, Barrett wrote, "The paramedics arrived but couldn't revive Jimi. They carried him out on a stretcher to the ambulance, assuring Monika that he was going to be all right. Either lying in bed on his back or on the way to the hospital, Jimi threw up on himself. The post-mortem concluded that Jimi had died of asphyxia while intoxicated with barbiturates."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Monika Dannemann is seen here outside the building where Jimi Hendrix died. (Brian Aris/Mirrorpix)

"... I flashed back to the time I took too much Mandrax, and my girlfriend couldn't wake me up," he wrote. "It was easily done and could've happened to any of us in Jimi's group of friends. That it happened to Jimi himself was heartbreaking. But I've never heard anything to make me think Jimi's death was anything other than what it appeared."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix is seen here with Eric Barrett at Heathrow Airport after flying in from New York on his way to the Isle of Wight pop festival. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Barrett firmly rejected the rumors and conspiracy theories that have surrounded Hendrix's death for decades. Among them was an allegation by former roadie James "Tappy" Wright, who wrote in his 2009 memoir, "Rock Roadie," that Hendrix’s manager, Mike Jeffery, confessed to killing Hendrix, The Guardian reported.
Barrett strongly disputes Wright's account and rejects any suggestion that Hendrix was murdered.
Manager Michael "Mike" Jeffery is seen outside Marylebone Register Office in June 1965. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

"I don't believe for a second that Mike Jeffery was the cause of Jimi's death," he said. "I just don't believe it. The circumstances don't add up. And I was told by so many people that Tappy only wrote that to try and sell books. But I've never believed it. I will never believe it. I was there, and right now I'm probably the last man standing. All the lads are passing. So no, I wouldn't believe that for a second."
Jeffery died in a plane crash near Nantes, France, in 1973.
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett are seen here at the Hollywood Bowl. (Chris Boyd)

Dannemann died in an apparent suicide in 1996, two days after she was found guilty of contempt of court in a long-running legal dispute with Kathy Etchingham, another former girlfriend of Hendrix's. She was 50.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
German painter and former figure skater Monika Dannemann holds a palette and brush as she works on one of her paintings in London, England, circa 1970. (Getty Images)
Barrett said that shortly after Hendrix's death, he lied to reporters about Hendrix's drug use.

"I was, what, 24 when he passed?" said Barrett. "I didn't want to besmirch his memory. So I lied. I just wanted people to see him in a good light. But I came to realize as I got older that I didn't have to lie. Yes, he took drugs. Did he take heroin? I've never seen heroin anywhere near him. I've worked on many backstages for almost 50 years. I know it's a drug that has killed a lot of musicians. But I don't believe Jimi was taking it. He smoked pot. He took a lot of LSD. He took pills. But I don't believe he was into heroin."
Eric Barrett watches over Jimi Hendrix as he performs in Zurich. (Johannes Bruell courtesy of the Marcel Aeby Collection)

Looking back, Barrett described Hendrix as "a wild man" on stage. The musician was famous for playing the guitar behind his head and with his teeth. He would also smash guitars and amps during encores and, on occasion, set his guitar on fire. But when the shows were over and audiences had long since left, Hendrix was a "quiet, mild-mannered, polite young man."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix plays his Fender Stratocaster with his teeth at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"He talked to everyone," he said. "He was very charming. And he was shy. People were in awe of Jimi. And when he had his guitar around his neck, over his shoulder, he was comfortable. That was his crutch. But I also remember Paul McCartney walking towards him, and he's gasping, 'It's Paul McCartney!' He was just a shy man who didn't know how to take the accolades of his talent."
"At the Shokan House before Woodstock, trying to teach a very stoned Jimi to ride," said Eric Barrett. (Willis Hogan Jr./David Pearcy Collection)

"I have so many memories of that wonderful man," Barrett continued. "I remember we were all staying in Benedict Canyon and it was my birthday. We were all hanging out by the pool, and Jimi came out in no shirt, just velvet pants. He goes, 'Eric, Eric!' I responded, 'Hey Jimi, what do you need?' He smiled and went, 'Happy birthday, man. Here's some money. Go and buy yourself something you really want.' He gave me $500, which was a huge amount back then."
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett at Benedict Canyon. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)

"I went to North Beach Leathers, a place I'd seen Jimi had bought some clothes from. I bought myself this long leather coat, spent all my money on it. It was the best gift I ever bought. When I came back, he loved it. He went, 'Wow, that's a coat! I wish I had seen that before you.'"

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix performs onstage with his Fender Stratocaster electric guitar at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Barrett said he carries "beautiful memories" of Hendrix. One in particular has never left him.

"With Jimi at TTG Studios in Los Angeles," said Eric Barrett. "He replaced my tambourine with a beer." (Michael Ochs)

"I was on a plane with him after a show," he said. "Jimi looked at me and said, 'Eric, what do you think, will they remember me?' I was flabbergasted. I went, 'Will they remember you? You're huge over here.' But he was so insecure. 'Are you sure, Eric? What if the kids don't come?' I just told him, 'When it comes to success, you have nothing to worry about.' title: Country duo Dan + Shay nearly broke up at height of success when their communication faltered
summary: Dan + Shay reveal the late-night conversation at Dan Smyers' home that saved their partnership after a 2021 communication breakdown nearly ended it all.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Country music duo Dan + Shay revealed they almost went their separate ways at the height of their success.

The duo, composed of Dan Smyers, 39, and Shay Mooney, 34, admitted while on the "Artist Friendly" podcast recently that, at the pinnacle of their success, "there was unhealthy dynamics between both of us 'cause we process things a lot differently."
Mooney explained that their biggest issue was that there "was just a communication stop," and they eventually "got to this point" where it was "just getting really tough."

"We had that moment in 2021, and it was kind of like, all right, do we ride off into the sunset and celebrate our accomplishments or do, like, we have some maybe really hard conversations with each other and fix this?" Mooney said.
The country music duo said they almost broke up at the height of their success. (David Becker/Getty Images)
COUNTRY STAR STEPS AWAY FROM MUSIC TO FOCUS ON HIMSELF AFTER FAME TOOK A TOLL

After host Joel Madden pressed the duo for more details, Smyers explained that, after they landed the opening slot for Kenny Chesney's tour, they were excited but didn't know if they could do it since their relationship was in a bad place.
They ultimately decided, "We have to figure this out," even if it meant that they "call it a day and go out on this Kenny tour as our farewell tour," Smyers said.
The two decided to meet at Smyers' home to have a conversation, with Smyers calling that meeting "the most pivotal critical moment in our entire career."
"We're either going to say peace out to this thing or we're going to figure this out and get it right," Mooney said.
Smyers added, "He ended up staying at the house till like 3, 4 in the morning and just hashing."
The duo had a meeting to discuss how they were going to move forward. (Sebron Snyder/Penske Media via Getty Images)

Mooney later explained that he felt as if Smyers wasn't enjoying himself during the shows, noting that he felt like he didn't "know how to make you enjoy these things" and that he just wanted his friend to be happy.

He was later able to understand that Smyers is particular about "those details that people don't see" and would get upset when things malfunction during shows, for instance, if "the video wall was out," whereas that isn't as big of an issue for Mooney.

"When we finally were like, 'Hey, you're not good at enjoying these things sometimes. I enjoy everything even when it's bad,'" Mooney said. "So, if we can meet somewhere in the middle, we can make this beautiful thing. Which is what happened in the beginning."

In the end, they chose to remain together as a duo after they both apologized for their part in the breakdown of their relationship. Smyers said they also established a new rule by which they let each other know when something is bothering them "rather than letting these things build up and boil and then it just explodes."

title: Comedian Leanne Morgan calls out Hollywood for living in a 'bubble' and misjudging what audiences want to see
summary: Comedian Leanne Morgan says Hollywood lives in a "bubble" and reveals she pushed back on a cursing scene while filming with Reese Witherspoon.

Comedian Leanne Morgan is calling out Hollywood for living in a "bubble."

During a recent appearance on "The Women of Joy Show" podcast, the 60-year-old actress discussed the idea that Christian women don't consume media with host Maegan Waldrep Schwindling, saying they want "quality" content but without "women in their panties shooting bows and arrows and all the things like it."

"Honest to goodness, I think in the secular world, I think people, no, I think a lot of people don't want to see all that," she said. "I think a lot of people don't want to see all that, and I think they're in a bubble out there. And they think people want to see that, but they're not in the middle of the United States."

She gave an example from when she was filming a movie with Reese Witherspoon and Will Ferrell in which she played a Southern mother of four who, in the script, was meant to curse in front of her children.
Morgan called out Hollywood for being in a "bubble." (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)
FORMER DISNEY STAR DAVID HENRIE REJECTED 'SECULAR' HOLLYWOOD LIFESTYLE AFTER LIFE-CHANGING MONASTERY VISIT

Morgan recalled telling the director that a Southern mother of four "wouldn't talk like that in front of these children." In that case, the director, Nick Stoller, told her, "You know better than I do, Leanne, and you do what you think is best."

"So I think they think in their minds, 'Oh, everybody's talking like this, everybody wants this,' but I don't think the majority of people do," she said. "Or not in the South, especially when you're portraying Southern characters. Or anywhere really."
She also explained that, growing up, no one in her family used swear words and while "it's OK if somebody else wants to use it," she doesn't care to use them herself.
The comedian is now starring in the Netflix show, "Leanne," in which she portrays a Southern mother in her 50s who is rebuilding her life after her husband left her for a younger woman.

In addition to making sure Southern Christians were not stereotyped on her show, she also felt the pressure to make sure the show was a success, saying she was reminded all the time how much it cost to make the show and how many people were relying on it.
"I've prayed more than I've ever prayed in my life," Morgan said.

title: Hilaria Baldwin explains how she stays fit raising 7 kids with ‘bathroom workouts’ and an unexpected diet
summary: Hilaria Baldwin shares her fitness routine, which includes bathroom workouts, while raising seven kids and pokes fun at Alec Baldwin for not being able to touch his toes.
story: The ‘Nation’s Dumbest’ star tells Fox News Digital how she prioritizes fitness while raising seven kids.
Hilaria Baldwin is taking the phrase "squeeze in a workout" to a whole new level.

The 42-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant and mother of seven told Fox News Digital her fitness routine doesn’t always happen in a gym or even in a dedicated workout space. Sometimes, it happens right there in the bathroom.

"I run every day. … I found being a mom, if I can get 30 minutes of my cardio, it helps my mind. ... It gets me, like, sort of a little bit more regulated with my nervous system, so I really like that," she shared when asked about her go-to workout with a hectic schedule.
HILARIA BALDWIN SHARES MARRIAGE LESSON SHE TELLS FRIENDS AFTER SURVIVING 'UPS AND OUR DOWNS' WITH ALEC BALDWIN
Hilaria Baldwin detailed the unconventional workout routine and diet habits she uses while raising seven children. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)
"Then I obviously do my yoga, my little bathroom workouts or just like a stop-and-drop little workout. I love Physique 57. Any kind of barre classes I think are really great."
And Hilaria isn’t just talking about quick bathroom sweat sessions.
Last month, she gave her fans a front-row look at exactly what those workouts can look like, showing off her physique in a bikini while demonstrating glute exercises in a bathroom.
Baldwin's routine included squats and leg raises.  (Hilaria Baldwin Instagram)
HILARIA BALDWIN FLAUNTS FIT FIGURE IN BIKINI AS FANS MARVEL AT MOM OF 7

"I think people think that I just eat salad all the time, which I’ve definitely done that in the past. But the other day — the baby of the family, we opened up pints of ice cream, two different pints of ice cream at 9 p.m. So, sometimes it looks like that.

When Fox News Digital asked if her husband, Alec Baldwin, ever joins her workouts, she laughed and said he’s not the most flexible person.
"Can’t touch his toes. I literally married the most inflexible person I have ever met."
Hilaria Baldwin competed on "Dancing with the Stars." (Getty Images)
'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS

title: Dolly Parton's path from Nashville newcomer to Billboard's No. 1 country music artist of all time
summary: Dolly Parton gained national attention in 1964 on "The Porter Wagoner Show," later becoming a 10-time Grammy Award winner and Academy Award nominee.
story: Steve Doocy joins 'Fox and Friends' to reflect on the life, career and charitable work of music icon Dolly Parton after her death at age 80. They discuss her music catalog, her Imagination Library literacy program and her Dollywood theme park in Tennessee.
Dolly Parton's career as an entertainer spanned roughly seven decades.
During that time, the legendary country music star cemented herself as an icon not only in the music industry, but also as a movie star and a philanthropist.

From getting her start on "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1964 to multiple Academy Award nominations, Parton forged a path for herself in the industry and paved the way for female country singers who followed her.
DOLLY PARTON’S SIX-DECADE LOVE STORY WITH CARL DEAN BEGAN AT A LAUNDROMAT
Parton's career as an entertainer spanned roughly seven decades. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Here are some of Parton's career highlights.
"The Porter Wagoner Show"
Parton joined "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1967. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Parton moved to Nashville, Tennessee, in May 1964, the day after graduating from high school, to pursue a career in country music.

Three years later, she released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in February 1967, which caught the attention of singer Porter Wagoner. He then invited Parton to join him on his TV show, "The Porter Wagoner Show," a few months later, in September 1967.

Parton's time on the show provided her with national attention and established her as a recording artist. Her duets with Wagoner, starting with "The Last Thing on My Mind," became major country hits. Their partnership also earned Parton her first Grammy nomination in 1970.

In addition to her duets with Wagoner, she released many of her well-known songs during this era, including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "My Tennessee Mountain Home," "Just Because I'm a Woman" and many more.
After seven years on the show, Parton felt it was time to pursue a solo career, ultimately leaving the show in 1974.
Solo success
Parton left "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1974 and had a successful solo career. (Getty Images)
Shortly after leaving the show, Parton released "Love Is Like a Butterfly," which quickly climbed to the top of the Billboard country charts.
She continued releasing hit after hit, including "Here You Come Again," off the album with the same name, which earned her first Grammy Award win in 1979.

She had 26 songs reach No. 1 on the Billboard country charts, including "The Bargain Store," "Heartbreaker," "Starting Over Again," "Tennessee Homesick Blues" and "Why'd You Come in Here Lookin' Like That."
In addition to her own music, Parton found success covering other artists' songs in her own style, including "Stairway to Heaven," "The House of the Rising Sun," "Shine" and others.

"Yes, and they loved it. Robert’s been out on tour, so he’s been doing a lot of interviews," she told Hot Press in 2002 about Led Zeppelin singer Robert Plant's reaction to her "Stairway to Heaven" cover.

"And he seems to make mention of it a lot, I guess, because people are asking him about it, and he says something different every time, but he seems to like it. He says he really likes what I did with it, and that makes me feel good."
‘I Will Always Love You’
Parton wrote "I Will Always Love You" in 1973 for her friend, Porter Wagoner. (David Redfern/Redferns)
Parton wrote one of her most well-known songs, "I Will Always Love You," in 1973 when she told Wagoner she wanted to leave the show and go solo.

When Wagoner responded negatively and all her efforts to get him to understand her reasoning fell on deaf ears, Parton thought she would put all her feelings into a song and play it for him to help him understand.

"I said, ‘Porter, sit down. I got something I need to sing to you,’" she told Howard Stern in 2023. "He was just sitting behind his desk and tears started rolling down. He said, ‘That’s just the best song you ever wrote, and you can go if I can produce the song.’"

The song was released in 1974 as part of her "Jolene" album, and climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart. It returned to No. 1 again in 1982 when Parton released a different version for "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas."
Whitney Houston's version of the song spent 14 consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. (Fotos International/Getty Images)
Nearly two decades after the song's initial release, Whitney Houston's version reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, where it stayed for 14 consecutive weeks.
Houston recorded an R&B ballad version of the song for the soundtrack to "The Bodyguard."

In addition to staying at the No. 1 spot for 14 weeks, it was Billboard's No. 1 song of 1993, went 19 times platinum in the U.S., and won two Grammy Awards at the 1994 ceremony. This version of the song is also the highest-selling single written by a female artist.
"I almost wrecked, honest to god. I had to pull over to a Walgreens … and listen to the rest of it," Parton told Stern about hearing Houston's version for the first time.
"I couldn’t believe my little country sad song could even be done like that … and it was just overwhelming. That was one of the greatest experiences I ever had in my entire life."
‘Dolly!’ and ‘Dolly’ variety shows
Parton hosted two variety shows of her own, from 1976-1977 and from 1987-1988. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
Two years after leaving "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton started her own variety show called "Dolly!" in 1976.
The show aired 26 half-hour episodes and featured guest stars such as Kenny Rogers, Linda Ronstadt, Emmylou Harris, Anne Murray and many others.
Ten years after that show ended, she released a second variety show, "Dolly," in 1987.

The show aired 22 one-hour episodes from September 1987 to May 1988 and was a huge ratings success, featuring guests such as Oprah Winfrey, Bruce Willis and Loretta Lynn as well as Kermit the Frog and Miss Piggy.
Iconic collaborations
Parton and Rogers collaborated for the first time in 1983 with "Islands in the Stream." (Beth Gwinn/Redferns)
In addition to Wagoner, Parton had several other significant collaborations throughout her career.

One of her most celebrated partnerships was with Kenny Rogers. The two first connected in 1983 when they recorded the hit song "Islands In the Stream" together. The song was a massive crossover hit and spent two consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned them a Grammy nomination.
The two later released a joint Christmas album in 1984, "Once Upon a Christmas," and a year later collaborated on "Real Love," which reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot Country Singles chart.
Nearly 30 years later, they released "You Can't Make Old Friends" in 2013, the title track of Rogers' album with the same name, earning them another Grammy nomination.
Parton and Rogers reunited in 2013 for their duet "You Can't Make Old Friends." (Rick Diamond)

"It really made me very emotional," Parton told ABC News in September 2013 about the song. "Even when I was recording it, I was tearful, and when I was listening to the demo it really just, you know, it certainly summed us up and our relationship. But it also is such a song of friendship of all kinds."

Parton also partnered with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt in 1987 to release their highly successful album, "Trio," which largely featured covers, except for "Wildflowers," which was written by Parton for the album.
The album reached No. 1 on Billboard's country albums chart and No. 6 on the Billboard 200 and earned the three artists a Grammy.
They followed it with "Trio II" in 1999, which featured a highly praised cover of Neil Young's song "After the Gold Rush," which earned them yet another Grammy.
Parton also collaborated with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on two albums. (Paul Harris/Getty Images)
In addition to these collaborations, Parton released songs with Brad Paisley, Vince Gill, Willie Nelson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus and others.
Movie career
Parton made her feature film debut in 1980 in the comedy "9 to 5." (20th Century Fox/Getty Images)
After making a name for herself in the music world, she set her sights on movies.

Parton made her feature film debut in the 1980 classic comedy "9 to 5," which also starred Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Tomlin, Fonda and Parton played a trio of secretaries who took revenge on their sexist boss by kidnapping him and enacting changes in the workplace in his name.
The movie was an instant classic, earning Parton three Golden Globe nominations and an Oscar nomination for best original song for the song she wrote for the film, "9 to 5."

Two years later, Parton made a splash with a second critically-acclaimed role in the film "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," playing Miss Mona, a madam at the Chicken Ranch, a long-running Texas brothel.
Dolly Parton also starred in "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." (Universal Studios/YouTube)
Her role in the film earned her another Golden Globe nomination.
She then starred in the 1989 movie "Steel Magnolias," alongside Hollywood heavy hitters Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis and Julia Roberts.
Together, they portrayed a group of Southern women who banded together during life's good and hard moments, with Parton in particular playing a hair stylist.

"I totally related to her. She's not different from me at all, and it wasn't hard for me to play a Southern girl with a Southern accent," she told "Today" in 1989. "And it's not foreign to me, like you said in your intro, for me to do hair, 'cause I grew up doing my sister's hair, my friends' hair. I started cutting and bleaching in a salon on my own at 15 years old and I loved it."
Parton later starred in "Steel Magnolias." (Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images)

She also appeared in the films "Rhinestone," "Straight Talk," "The Beverly Hillbillies," "Miss Congeniality 2: Armed and Fabulous," "Joyful Noise" and others, including appearing on three episodes of "Hannah Montana."
Award wins and nominations
Parton won a Grammy for "There Was Jesus" and her first Emmy for "Christmas on the Square" in 2021 at the age of 75. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
Parton received many accolades during her roughly seven decades in the entertainment industry.

Since releasing her first album in 1967, Parton had received a total of 55 Grammy Award nominations, resulting in 10 wins. Her first win came in 1979 in the female country vocal performance for her song "Here You Come Again."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

She later won awards for "9 to 5," "Trio," "The Grass Is Blue," "Shine" and other projects, with her final nomination coming in 2025 for Best Audiobook Narration and Storytelling Recording for her memoir, "Behind The Seams: My Life In Rhinestones."

Her music was also celebrated in the film world, with two Academy Award nominations for best original song. The first came in 1981 for her song, "9 to 5," and the second in 2006 for the song, "Travelin' Thru," featured in the movie, "Transamerica."
Parton also won 10 CMA Awards, including Entertainer of the Year. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)

Parton received six Golden Globe nominations over her career, including three for "9 to 5" and one for her performance in "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." She also won an Emmy Award for outstanding television movie as an executive producer of "Christmas on the Square."
She also won 10 CMA Awards out of 45 nominations, including Entertainer of the Year in 1978, five ACM Awards and seven CMT Awards.
Recognition
Parton received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006. (Scott Suchman/WireImage)
Parton was honored in other ways, in addition to the many awards she accumulated throughout her career.
In 1984, the singer received her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999 and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001.
She later received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006, recognizing her contributions to American culture.
In 2022, Parton was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Two years later, Billboard named Parton the No. 1 country music artist of all time.
Parton was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for American Greetings)

"People usually [say] ‘Dolly rocks’ or ‘you rock’ or ‘you’re a rock star.’ I thought they just meant that I was cool, and I took that as a great compliment," she told Billboard in February 2022 about the induction. "But now I’m going to have to take it literally!"
Imagination Library
Parton started the Imagination Library in 1995. (Paul Natkin/Getty Images)
Apart from her work as an entertainer, Parton was also known for her philanthropy.

She started the Imagination Library in 1995, which sends free books to children around the world from birth to age 5, no matter their families' economic status. She was inspired to create the program by her father, who never learned to read or write.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
According to the organization's website, over 3 million kids have registered, and over 330 million books have been gifted since the program started.
"When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams," Parton said in a statement on the website.

"They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer. The seeds of these dreams are often found in books, and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world."
Dollywood
Parton opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in 1986. (Ron Davis/Getty Images)
Parton showed off her business knowledge when she opened her own theme park called Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, in 1986.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Not only was the theme park popular, drawing about 4 million visitors annually. It also provided job opportunities for thousands of people in the area, proving Parton was all about giving back to her community.

"The Smokies — and the wonderful people who work here — are what make Dollywood so different than many of the other theme parks around the world," she told National Geographic in January 2024, according to People.

"We’re right on the front porch of the most-visited national park in the country, so we take what God gave us and use it to dream up the big dreams we want our guests to experience while they are here riding rides and making memories."
Songs she wrote for others
Parton was a prolific songwriter who wrote songs for other artists often. (Ron Davis/Getty Images)
In addition to her own chart toppers, Parton wrote many songs for other artists that were also big hits.

Included in the list are "Kentucky Gambler," which she wrote for Merle Haggard and became a No. 1 country hit in 1975, and "Put It Off Until Tomorrow" for Bill Phillips, which became a top 10 country hit.

She also wrote "Waltz Me to Heaven" for Waylon Jennings, "The Stranger" for Kenny Rogers," "I'm In No Condition" for Hank Williams Jr., "Love, You’re So Beautiful Tonight" for Willie Nelson and "There'll Always Be Music" for Tina Turner.
These are far from all the songs she wrote. It's been reported that Parton had a catalog of over 3,000 songs penned by her.
