title: Minnesota Supreme Court rejects Mike Lindell’s bid to recount GOP primary
summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election.
story: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election. Now, he’s refusing to accept his own election loss in the GOP primary for governor of Minnesota.
The Minnesota Supreme Court on Saturday rejected Lindell’s bid for a full recount of his Aug. 11 loss to state House Speaker Lisa Demuth after she won the Republican primary by 45,000 votes.

Chief Justice Natalie E. Hudson wrote in a six-page ruling that the Minnesota secretary of state’s office and its State Canvassing Board provided a recount plan that follows the law and are “not committing any wrongful act, omission, or error” as Lindell claimed.

Lindell told NBC News in a phone call Saturday evening that he plans to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. He said that his team is also requesting election data from all 87 counties through the Freedom of Information Act in order to pursue an independent investigation.
“I’m willing to pay even more money. I don’t care what it costs,” Lindell said.

Lindell previously pledged to pay an estimated $825,000 to cover a full hand recount and audit of the race but refused to pay the money on Monday, the state’s deadline, after finding out that the recount only included counting the ballots cast for either Lindell or Demuth.

Lindell sued the Minnesota secretary of state’s office and its State Canvassing Board Monday, claiming that they pulled a “bait-and-switch” on him by not counting the ballots for everyone in the seven-candidate Republican field.

The secretary of state’s office said in a statement Tuesday that it provided the contingent recount plan to Lindell after the State Canvassing Board approved it on Aug. 18, writing that “the plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans.”

Hudson acknowledged in her ruling that Lindell argued “he is entitled to a full recount for both the Democratic and Republican primary races for governor ‘to ensure that there are no anomalies in the ballots, whether the votes cast are for the Democratic or Republican primaries,’ and that this recount must include ‘the recording of votes for every candidate.’”
“But Lindell’s focus on alleged anomalies confuses the purpose of a manual recount with an election contest,” Hudson wrote.

Hudson maintained that the recount plan approved by the canvassing board on Aug. 18 follows protocol, saying that during the recount, the ballots would first be sorted between those cast in the Democratic or the Republican primary and then the Republican ballots would be separated into three piles: one for Lindell, one for Demuth and one for all other candidates.

“In other words, after all votes are sorted and counted, Lindell would know whether he is the winner over Demuth,” Hudson wrote. “And all ballots, in all piles, would be counted and subject to challenge.”
Hudson’s ruling backs up Demuth’s victory in the GOP primary, reinforcing her spot in the general election against Democratic nominee, Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Lindell said Saturday he would not be satisfied with anything less than a full hand recount of all ballots cast in the Minnesota gubernatorial primary races, arguing that there were “anomalies” in the election data due to the use of electronic voting machines.
Before his own gubernatorial campaign, Lindell faced multiple lawsuits after he repeated debunked claims that the 2020 election was rigged by voting machines.
Lindell was found to have defamed a former employee of one company, Dominion Voting Systems, in June 2025. Lindell has denied the claim.

In another defamation case, Lindell has refused to pay $56,369 in sanctions to voting machine company Smartmatic USA Corp. Because he still has not paid what the court ordered, Lindell now owes even more than the original sanctions in court fees. He told NBC News this month that he still does not intend to pay either the fees or sanctions.

title: Iran’s supreme leader urges Gulf rulers to confront ‘real enemy’ in written message
summary: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
story: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
The ⁠message was published on Khamenei’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad.
It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who ⁠creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” ​helps ⁠Islam’s enemies.
It asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” if Muslims had been united.

Khamenei has not ⁠been seen in public since being injured in U.S.-Israeli airstrikes six ​months ⁠ago that launched the ‌Iran war, killing his father and previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

His call for unity echoes a statement he made ‌on Friday to Iranians, when he said ‌he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale.

Khamenei specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers ⁠whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.”

Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Gulf Arab monarchies have viewed Iran’s revolutionary ideology, including its anti-monarchic rhetoric and regional influence, as a threat to their ‌political systems.
During the present conflict, Tehran has struck ​U.S. military facilities as well as other infrastructure in ‌Gulf states, underscoring the tensions ⁠between Tehran and its Gulf neighbours.

“My emphatic and repeated recommendation ⁠to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia ‌and the Gulf, is ​to identify your real enemy, ‌understand his plan and confront it,” ​Khamenei said.
War weighs on Iran’s economy

Iranian leaders have acknowledged the economic toll of war with the U.S., with the supreme leader urging the government to ​address the hardship and the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by a third due to the American sanctions and blockade.

Yet Tehran signalled no retreat on Saturday, ‌vowing to withstand U.S. pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it said was control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets.

The government said in a statement on state media that addressing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war was a central focus, including curbing inflation, managing markets, creating jobs, directing investment towards domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.

Six months after the U.S. and ​Israel launched the war, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”.
President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.

Later on Saturday, Pezeshkian called on state TV for a revival of the interim deal, which was signed on June 17 but quickly unravelled amid disagreements over what had been agreed, especially ​on the status of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We ​can solve our problems and gain our ⁠privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said of a document that had offered Iran, among other things, immediate relief from U.S. sanctions and the release of its frozen assets.

title: Milo Yiannopoulos deported to the U.K. one day after ICE arrest
summary: Milo Yiannopoulos, a controversy-baiting internet personality who once vehemently backed President Donald Trump, has been deported to the United Kingdom, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said on Saturday.
story: Milo Yiannopoulos, a controversy-baiting internet personality who once vehemently backed President Donald Trump, has been deported to the United Kingdom, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said on Saturday.
Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on Friday after officials said he failed to show up for an immigration hearing in July.
DHS said that a final removal order was issued by an immigration judge on July 22.
ICE agents are increasingly making immigration-related arrests at airports.

Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian who was an early supporter of Trump’s political career, has worked with other MAGA-aligned figures and conspiracy theorists like Ye, formerly Kanye West, since his public parting from Trump’s inner circle.
Ye, who has come under fire in recent years for a series of antisemitic statements, performed at the New Orleans Caesars Superdome on Friday evening.
It is not clear whether Yiannopoulos was in New Orleans for the concert.
Yiannopoulos served as a tech editor at Breitbart, a conservative website, until February 2017, according the site.

Yiannopoulos resigned at that time following backlash over comments he’d made suggesting he supported certain adult relationships with children. In those comments, the openly gay agitator discussed the value of “cross-generational relationships.”

“And I think particularly in the gay world, and outside the Catholic Church — if that’s where some of you want to go with this — I think in the gay world some of the most important, enriching and incredibly life-affirming, important shaping relationships very often between younger boys and older men,” Yiannopoulos said in a past video clip.
“They can be hugely positive experiences.”
He also remarked that sexual abuse is “not the worst thing that’s ever going to happen to you ... going bankrupt is worse.”
Yiannopoulos was disinvited from speaking at a Conservative Political Action Conference around that time in the wake of those inflammatory remarks.
He later apologized and said he didn’t advocate for illegal behavior. He said he was sexually abused himself as a teen by two older men.

The Trump administration on Friday publicized Yiannopoulos’ arrest to help promote its voluntary deportation program. DHS is offering undocumented immigrants $3,000 and a free flight home for self-deportation.

“Being in detention is a choice,” DHS wrote on X, above Yiannopoulos’ haggard-looking mug shot. “We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the [Customs and Border Patrol] Home App.”

Conspiracy-peddler Laura Loomer, who is close to Trump and who has claimed responsibility for a number of firings and criminal investigations, took credit for reporting Yiannopoulos to ICE in a social media post.

title: Man posed as San Francisco 49er to defraud women of $1.3 million in multistate romance scheme, feds say
summary: A man was accused of pretending to be a San Francisco 49ers player to defraud women, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Oregon.
story: A man was accused of pretending to be a San Francisco 49ers player to defraud women, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Oregon.

Beginning in February 2022, Daejon Labrayae Love, 35, and Taylor Jamie Chan, 18, created fictitious investments to defraud numerous women in Oregon, Washington, Idaho and California, according to court documents.
Authorities said both men were arrested when Chan flew from California on Monday to meet Love in Boise, Idaho. Both were charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud.

Love would meet most of the women through dating apps and pretend to have a lavish lifestyle on social media, falsely portraying himself as a 49ers player or a wealthy real estate investor, according to authorities.

The attorney’s office said Love convinced victims they were in sincere romantic relationships with him, that he was a sophisticated investor and that Chan was his “investment adviser,” who helped Love to grow a fortune of tens of millions of dollars.

Love told the victims he wanted to build wealth and a future with them, authorities said. Officials added Love advertised nonexistent investment vehicles, claiming these investments would generate massive returns for both him and his victims.
Court documents said Love used phone apps to create fictitious bank and investment accounts and balances to show the victims and make the scheme appear legitimate.

Authorities said Love and Chan exchanged electronic communications in which Chan pretended to be Love’s investment adviser and would send messages encouraging Love to invest in new opportunities. Love would then send screenshots of those messages to the victims to convince them to send money to either of them, according to court documents.

The U.S. attorney’s office said the pair would have video calls with the victims to show them falsified investment gains and encourage them to part with their money. If the victims did not have money, authorities said, Love sometimes instructed them to take a loan; if they were left with no more money to invest or asked too many questions, Love would block them, stop any communication with them and keep the money.
Financial records show the pair received about $1.3 million from victims, according to authorities. Officials said 26 victims have been identified, but the FBI believes there could be more.
The FBI encourages anyone with information on Love or Chan to submit a tip at the FBI website https://tips.fbi.gov/home or to call 1-800-CALL-FBI.

title: Water cuts are coming for Arizona. Is your salad on the chopping block?
summary: Yuma County, Arizona grows 90% of the U.S.’ winter salad greens. But the state relies on the depleted Colorado River, and water cuts are about to hit.
story: The Colorado River fills America’s salad bowl. It’s a vital source of water to Yuma County, Arizona, which grows 90% of the leafy greens the country consumes in the winter — but it’s nearing a crisis point.
With the river’s water levels at record lows, Arizona is poised to take the biggest cuts: about 30% of its Colorado River supply in 2027 and 2028.

Those are the terms stipulated by the Bureau of Reclamation, which imposed a mandatory two-year plan after the seven states that use Colorado River water failed to reach an agreement. If the megadrought persists and water levels continue to fall, a 10-year management plan the bureau has proposed would allow even harsher cuts that could threaten the country’s winter greens.

“If you cut us off at the knees, or if you restrict the water, it has a national impact,” said Jonathan Lines, a member of the Yuma County Board of Supervisors. “It’s a national security issue and a food security issue.”

Arizona’s agriculture is one rather large ripple of the Colorado River crisis, whose full scale is almost impossible to grasp. About 40 million people in Western states rely on the river for drinking water, but it is shrinking from overuse, drought and climate change. Utilities also depend on it to generate electricity at the dams on Lake Mead and Lake Powell, where much of the water is stored, but both reservoirs hit record lows this month.

title: Fears of more flooding in Nepal, 100 Americans among the missing as rescue efforts step up
summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Authorities in Nepal have warned of the risk of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region.
story: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Authorities in Nepal have warned of the risk of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region.

Five days after surging floodwaters from a glacier collapse buried communities across the region in thick mud, rescuers in Nepal were still struggling to reach devastated communities as the full scale of the destruction emerged.

“The disaster here is overwhelming,” Ferrin Cole, an operations director at the U.S.-based Crisis Response International, told NBC News on Sunday. “The flood that came down that mountain just wiped out cities. We’re going in as fast as we can to get people the help that they need.”
Cole said his team would be working to help locate missing persons, but that working in mud “is actually pretty dangerous.”
“The longer that death and mud are together, diseases breed, and so we’re always just aware of that,” he added.
Approximately 100 Americans are among the missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region, the State Department said Saturday.
How did the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet flood happen?

In Nepal, the death toll has risen to 781, with over 2,500 people still missing, including 592 foreign nationals, according to the country’s disaster agency. The Nepal Tourism Board said 289 foreign nationals have been rescued.

China has separately reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in its Tibet region, including 261 foreign nationals. It is unclear how much overlap there is between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts.

Those missing loved ones may face a long wait for answers, with many bodies washed far downstream and recovered in poor condition. Morgues in Nepal have been overwhelmed, though authorities are collecting DNA samples in the hopes of notifying relatives.
In Nepal’s Chitwan district, where a number of bodies have washed up, police officer Anil Thapa told Reuters that “more than half” of recovered bodies were “beyond recognition.”
“Many have no visible faces. In some cases, only hands or legs remain,” the officer added.

The response is also being complicated by a landslide-dammed lake above the border checkpoint that is overflowing, while heavy rain in Nepal has pushed up river levels and prompted fresh warnings for people living along waterways.
Nepal’s flood alert system said Sunday that heavy rainfall had been measured in various watershed areas of Gandaki province, and that the water levels were “expected to rise.”
“Therefore, people living in riverside areas are requested to adopt caution,” it said on X.
But in flood-hit areas, residents were struggling to make sense of repeated warnings since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” Govind Shreshta, a resident of the town of Galchhi, told The Associated Press. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

Chinese state-run media outlet CCTV said Sunday that the event was part of a growing pattern of glacier-related disasters in the region, with the avalanche reaching China’s Gyirong Port within minutes of occurring.
“The disaster was caused by glacier instability resulting from the long-term effects of climate warming,” said Chinese state media.

“It struck suddenly, with a large peak flow, high speed, severe destructive force and a wide impact area,” the report added. “These are also new and significant characteristics of cryosphere-related disasters emerging across the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding regions.”
While it will take time to determine the exact cause of the mudslide and flood disaster, analysts say climate change likely played a role.

The Himalayan region, which includes Nepal, India, Pakistan, Bhutan, China and Afghanistan, is among the places most vulnerable to climate change, with temperatures rising faster than the global average. The warmer conditions are accelerating glacial melt, further destabilizing a region that is already prone to floods, landslides and earthquakes.
The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake.

The U.S. Geological Survey later revised that number to the equivalent of a magnitude-5.2 earthquake and said a second seismic event three hours after the first registered as the equivalent of a 4.2 temblor. Debris flow and flooding from what it called a “slope failure” traveled 62 miles, the USGS said.

“We will not be able to attribute 100% that this is because of climate change, because these changes have been happening” over a long period of time, Neera Shrestha Pradhan, an expert at Nepal’s International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, said on Friday. But climate change might be breaking a threshold, she said, and “maybe that might be one of the causes of this happening.”
Janis Mackey Frayer, Dawn Liu and Sunil Pandey reported from Kathmandu, Nepal. Freddie Clayton reported from London.

title: Iran’s supreme leader urges Gulf rulers to confront ‘real enemy’ in written message
summary: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
story: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
The ⁠message was published on Khamenei’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad.
It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who ⁠creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” ​helps ⁠Islam’s enemies.
It asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” if Muslims had been united.

Khamenei has not ⁠been seen in public since being injured in U.S.-Israeli airstrikes six ​months ⁠ago that launched the ‌Iran war, killing his father and previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

His call for unity echoes a statement he made ‌on Friday to Iranians, when he said ‌he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale.

Khamenei specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers ⁠whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.”

Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Gulf Arab monarchies have viewed Iran’s revolutionary ideology, including its anti-monarchic rhetoric and regional influence, as a threat to their ‌political systems.
During the present conflict, Tehran has struck ​U.S. military facilities as well as other infrastructure in ‌Gulf states, underscoring the tensions ⁠between Tehran and its Gulf neighbours.

“My emphatic and repeated recommendation ⁠to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia ‌and the Gulf, is ​to identify your real enemy, ‌understand his plan and confront it,” ​Khamenei said.
War weighs on Iran’s economy

Iranian leaders have acknowledged the economic toll of war with the U.S., with the supreme leader urging the government to ​address the hardship and the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by a third due to the American sanctions and blockade.

Yet Tehran signalled no retreat on Saturday, ‌vowing to withstand U.S. pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it said was control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets.

The government said in a statement on state media that addressing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war was a central focus, including curbing inflation, managing markets, creating jobs, directing investment towards domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.

Six months after the U.S. and ​Israel launched the war, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”.
President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.

Later on Saturday, Pezeshkian called on state TV for a revival of the interim deal, which was signed on June 17 but quickly unravelled amid disagreements over what had been agreed, especially ​on the status of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We ​can solve our problems and gain our ⁠privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said of a document that had offered Iran, among other things, immediate relief from U.S. sanctions and the release of its frozen assets.

title: Minnesota Supreme Court rejects Mike Lindell’s bid to recount GOP primary
summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election.
story: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell has long denied Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 presidential election. Now, he’s refusing to accept his own election loss in the GOP primary for governor of Minnesota.
The Minnesota Supreme Court on Saturday rejected Lindell’s bid for a full recount of his Aug. 11 loss to state House Speaker Lisa Demuth after she won the Republican primary by 45,000 votes.

Chief Justice Natalie E. Hudson wrote in a six-page ruling that the Minnesota secretary of state’s office and its State Canvassing Board provided a recount plan that follows the law and are “not committing any wrongful act, omission, or error” as Lindell claimed.

Lindell told NBC News in a phone call Saturday evening that he plans to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. He said that his team is also requesting election data from all 87 counties through the Freedom of Information Act in order to pursue an independent investigation.
“I’m willing to pay even more money. I don’t care what it costs,” Lindell said.

Lindell previously pledged to pay an estimated $825,000 to cover a full hand recount and audit of the race but refused to pay the money on Monday, the state’s deadline, after finding out that the recount only included counting the ballots cast for either Lindell or Demuth.

Lindell sued the Minnesota secretary of state’s office and its State Canvassing Board Monday, claiming that they pulled a “bait-and-switch” on him by not counting the ballots for everyone in the seven-candidate Republican field.

The secretary of state’s office said in a statement Tuesday that it provided the contingent recount plan to Lindell after the State Canvassing Board approved it on Aug. 18, writing that “the plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans.”

Hudson acknowledged in her ruling that Lindell argued “he is entitled to a full recount for both the Democratic and Republican primary races for governor ‘to ensure that there are no anomalies in the ballots, whether the votes cast are for the Democratic or Republican primaries,’ and that this recount must include ‘the recording of votes for every candidate.’”
“But Lindell’s focus on alleged anomalies confuses the purpose of a manual recount with an election contest,” Hudson wrote.

Hudson maintained that the recount plan approved by the canvassing board on Aug. 18 follows protocol, saying that during the recount, the ballots would first be sorted between those cast in the Democratic or the Republican primary and then the Republican ballots would be separated into three piles: one for Lindell, one for Demuth and one for all other candidates.

“In other words, after all votes are sorted and counted, Lindell would know whether he is the winner over Demuth,” Hudson wrote. “And all ballots, in all piles, would be counted and subject to challenge.”
Hudson’s ruling backs up Demuth’s victory in the GOP primary, reinforcing her spot in the general election against Democratic nominee, Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Lindell said Saturday he would not be satisfied with anything less than a full hand recount of all ballots cast in the Minnesota gubernatorial primary races, arguing that there were “anomalies” in the election data due to the use of electronic voting machines.
Before his own gubernatorial campaign, Lindell faced multiple lawsuits after he repeated debunked claims that the 2020 election was rigged by voting machines.
Lindell was found to have defamed a former employee of one company, Dominion Voting Systems, in June 2025. Lindell has denied the claim.

In another defamation case, Lindell has refused to pay $56,369 in sanctions to voting machine company Smartmatic USA Corp. Because he still has not paid what the court ordered, Lindell now owes even more than the original sanctions in court fees. He told NBC News this month that he still does not intend to pay either the fees or sanctions.

title: Four baby goats at mobile petting zoo in North Carolina test positive for rabies
summary: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment.
story: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment.

The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said anyone who had contact with the baby goats at Farm Adventures’ location in Harmony, North Carolina, or at one of its mobile events between July 28 and Thursday should contact local health officials.
“The petting zoo held off-site events involving children and elderly individuals across multiple counties within that time frame,” the department said.
Health professionals may determine whether people who had contact with the baby goats need further examination or precautionary medication, it said.
Without it, rabies is almost always fatal in humans, the state health department said.
Farm Adventures said in a statement posted to Facebook that it is monitoring its other animals for signs of the viral disease.
“The affected animals, our four precious baby goats, have been euthanized to prevent further spread,” it said.
The baby goats were too young for vaccination and were bitten by a skunk that was found in their separate pen, the petting zoo said.
It said it was unaware the goats had been bitten, and that they did not show typical symptoms of the disease. After the first goat’s death, the petting zoo sent its body to be tested, it said.
It was unclear when the skunk was found in the pen.
Skunks are one of the animals most often found with rabies, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

People can get rabies through pets, wild animals and other humans through a bite, a scratch or even infected saliva, it said.  It can take weeks after exposure for early symptoms to begin, including flulike illness, feeling weak, fevers, headaches and a prickling or itching sensation, health officials say.
North Carolina hasn’t had a reported human case since 2011, the state health department said.
Roughly 100,000 Americans a year receive a rabies vaccine following a potential exposure, according to the CDC. It characterizes rabies as “a rare but serious public health concern.”
The petting zoo said it’s cooperating with state and local government officials.

“We are working closely with public health officials, the North Carolina Department of Agriculture, and animal control to address this issue and ensure the safety of our animals and clients,” it said in its statement.
The petting zoo, responding to a comment on Facebook, said it’s hoping its customers are unaffected.
“I am truly concerned about anyone that has been able to enjoy our animals,” the comment said. “We would NEVER intend to put anyone in danger.”
NBC News has reached out to the petting zoo for additional comment.

title: Taylor Swift donates $50,000 to mother who was seriously injured in car accident
summary: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in a car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed.
story: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in a car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed.

Ashley Taunton, a married mother of three, was driving on I-95 in Hopkinton during a torrential rainstorm on July 18 when she saw a car in front of her hydroplane off the road. She pulled over and ran to help the teenagers inside the crashed vehicle, her husband, Joe Taunton, told NBC affiliate WJAR of Providence.
As she was helping them, another vehicle hydroplaned and barreled toward them, he said.
“In a split-second act of pure bravery, Ashley pushed the other person out of harm’s way, taking the brunt of the impact herself,” according to an online fundraiser to support her medical bills.

Joe Taunton said his wife suffered a severe leg injury and extensive internal injuries, including damage to her small and large intestines, liver lacerations and a ruptured diaphragm that caused one of her lungs to collapse. She has undergone at least three surgeries, he said.

Ashley Taunton has documented her recovery on social media, sharing photos of her in a hospital bed in an induced coma, with a nasogastric tube for a small bowel obstruction, staples on her stomach, and — more recently — back home in a leg brace.
On Friday, she posted on Instagram about Swift’s donation, writing: “This is absolutely mind-blowing and so very humbling.”

“@taylorswift you are a beautiful soul I wish I could hug you IRL. Maybe the next time your in Westerly 😘 I live 20 minutes away 🫶 Thank you Jesus for so many amazing humans. This is unbelievable and I am overwhelmed with gratitude. To God be the glory!” she wrote.

title: Palestinian woman and NBC News team attacked by masked Israeli settlers in West Bank
summary: Masked Israeli settlers attacked and injured a Palestinian woman and members of an NBC News team reporting in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday.
story: Masked Israeli settlers attacked and injured a Palestinian woman and members of an NBC News team reporting in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday.

Three members of an NBC team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus, when the attack occurred. Abdullah said they had been driven out of their home by Israeli settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.
A gray car with Israeli license plates then drove in reverse up the hill toward them, video of the incident shows.

A masked man in a blue tracksuit, holding a stick, was leaning out of the rear passenger window as the vehicle approached. When the car stopped, at least four men in dark clothes and with their faces covered leaped out, hitting Abdullah and the crew with sticks and throwing rocks at them.
“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News international correspondent Matt Bradley, who was hit twice in the arm and later treated at a nearby clinic.

Abdullah, 51, who was on the ground after the attack, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening, according to an Israeli military and Israel Border Police statement. According to her husband, Mahmoud Toubasi, Abdullah’s condition had improved but she remained in the hospital Saturday night.
Two additional members of the NBC News team — a cameraman and producer — were also injured and were treated following the attack.
Producer Lawahez Jabari described how the car rushed up the hill before its occupants beat members of the team and damaged camera equipment and one of the crew’s vehicles.
“Suddenly a car came to us,” she said after receiving medical care. “The settlers had sticks. I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”
Camera operator Khaldoon Eid, who lives in the West Bank, said he was surprised the attack occurred in the middle of the village.
“We didn’t expect that — that they would come to attack,” he said. “We were in the middle of a Palestinian area next to Palestinian houses.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his spokesman Doron Spielman condemned the violence against Abdullah and the NBC News crew along with several other incidents across the area on Saturday.
Those incidents included dozens of masked Israeli settlers spraying pepper spray at Palestinian workers and throwing rocks at a building in nearby Qusra.

Netanyahu said the “criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Kosra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world.”

Spielman said in a post on X that “their actions violate the law; they endanger both Jews and Arabs, and they interfere with the Israel Defense Forces as they carry out vital security missions, and of course they harm Israel’s international legitimacy.”
Netanyahu, he said, requested that security forces “apprehend the perpetrators and to bring them to justice,” adding Israel “will not tolerate vigilantism of any kind by anyone.”

Israeli security described the regional violence on Saturday, saying they received reports that “rioters had arrived in the area and that violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians.”
“Upon their arrival, the security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside,” the statement said.

“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.
“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.
There has been a spate of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, and the village of Qusra has been besieged by Israeli settlers for weeks.

Between Jan. 1 and July 24, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians, according to the latest data available from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. Three Israelis were killed over the same period, the data shows.

Netanyahu’s hard-line government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks in the West Bank, which many governments around the world consider illegally occupied. In its statement after the attack, Israeli security forces said they “strongly condemn all forms of violence.”
Captured in the 1967 Middle East war, the West Bank is home to 3 million Palestinians and 500,000 Israeli settlers.

The recent escalation in violence has increased pressure on the Israeli military to stop these armed groups. The United Nations and media workers have also reported an uptick in attacks on foreign, Palestinian and Israeli journalists in the West Bank.

title: Milo Yiannopoulos deported to the U.K. one day after ICE arrest
summary: Milo Yiannopoulos, a controversy-baiting internet personality who once vehemently backed President Donald Trump, has been deported to the United Kingdom, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said on Saturday.
story: Milo Yiannopoulos, a controversy-baiting internet personality who once vehemently backed President Donald Trump, has been deported to the United Kingdom, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said on Saturday.
Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on Friday after officials said he failed to show up for an immigration hearing in July.
DHS said that a final removal order was issued by an immigration judge on July 22.
ICE agents are increasingly making immigration-related arrests at airports.

Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian who was an early supporter of Trump’s political career, has worked with other MAGA-aligned figures and conspiracy theorists like Ye, formerly Kanye West, since his public parting from Trump’s inner circle.
Ye, who has come under fire in recent years for a series of antisemitic statements, performed at the New Orleans Caesars Superdome on Friday evening.
It is not clear whether Yiannopoulos was in New Orleans for the concert.
Yiannopoulos served as a tech editor at Breitbart, a conservative website, until February 2017, according the site.

Yiannopoulos resigned at that time following backlash over comments he’d made suggesting he supported certain adult relationships with children. In those comments, the openly gay agitator discussed the value of “cross-generational relationships.”

“And I think particularly in the gay world, and outside the Catholic Church — if that’s where some of you want to go with this — I think in the gay world some of the most important, enriching and incredibly life-affirming, important shaping relationships very often between younger boys and older men,” Yiannopoulos said in a past video clip.
“They can be hugely positive experiences.”
He also remarked that sexual abuse is “not the worst thing that’s ever going to happen to you ... going bankrupt is worse.”
Yiannopoulos was disinvited from speaking at a Conservative Political Action Conference around that time in the wake of those inflammatory remarks.
He later apologized and said he didn’t advocate for illegal behavior. He said he was sexually abused himself as a teen by two older men.

The Trump administration on Friday publicized Yiannopoulos’ arrest to help promote its voluntary deportation program. DHS is offering undocumented immigrants $3,000 and a free flight home for self-deportation.

“Being in detention is a choice,” DHS wrote on X, above Yiannopoulos’ haggard-looking mug shot. “We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the [Customs and Border Patrol] Home App.”

Conspiracy-peddler Laura Loomer, who is close to Trump and who has claimed responsibility for a number of firings and criminal investigations, took credit for reporting Yiannopoulos to ICE in a social media post.

title: Suspected Florida cinnamon roll bandit wasn’t a thief — he was detained by immigration agents, bakery says
summary: The case of an Uber courier accused of disappearing with thousands of dollars’ worth of cinnamon rolls in South Florida has taken a turn.
story: The case of an Uber courier accused of disappearing with thousands of dollars’ worth of cinnamon rolls in South Florida has taken a turn.

Julie Pierre, founder of South Florida-based viral bakery business Roll and Dough, initially believed the driver she hired to deliver 400 cinnamon rolls to a farmers’ market took off with the pastries after they never made it to their destination on Saturday.
The 21-year-old took to social media on Thursday to say that she finally got the real story.

“Based on the limited information available to us at the time, we believed our cinnamon rolls had been stolen,” Roll and Dough said in a statement posted on Instagram. “Uber instructed us to file a police report, so we followed their guidance.”
“We did not know that the carrier, Ivan, had been detained by immigration authorities during the delivery,” the statement continued.
Sunrise Police confirmed the driver was taken into custody by U.S. Border Patrol (CBP) in Hollywood while he was en route to deliver the cinnamon rolls.

In a statement, a CBP spokesperson said the driver, Ivan Dario Rico Molano, was stopped at around 8:50 a.m. on Interstate 95 southbound near Sheridan Street “following a records check on a silver Kia Carnival.”

“The registered owner was identified as an alien without legal immigration status. During the encounter, the driver, identified as Ivan Dario Rico Molano, a citizen of Colombia, admitted to being in the United States without legal authorization,” the spokesperson said. “Mr. Molano was arrested and transported to the Dania Beach Border Patrol Station for processing. Records indicate he entered the United States legally in May 2021, but remained beyond his authorized period of stay.”
Rico Molano then contacted someone to take the vehicle, which had the storage containers with Roll and Dough’s cinnamon rolls inside, police said.
Pierre said a family member of the driver found the cinnamon rolls and returned them to the police station, where Roll and Dough were able to recover them.

“Based on what we now know, Ivan did not intentionally steal our cinnamon rolls. We are sincerely sorry that we described the situation that way before learning the complete circumstances,” the statement read. “We shared what we genuinely understood at the time, and now that detectives have provided us with new information, we are publicly correcting the record.”
The business also said they wanted to donate a portion of their proceeds to help the driver’s family and cover any legal fees.

Some early Labor Day sales have already started, but the majority of them begin between Tuesday, Sept. 1 and Friday, Sept. 4. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales will be live by Sept. 4.

Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.”

All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend.

Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you.

Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.

title: Water cuts are coming for Arizona. Is your salad on the chopping block?
summary: Yuma County, Arizona grows 90% of the U.S.’ winter salad greens. But the state relies on the depleted Colorado River, and water cuts are about to hit.
story: The Colorado River fills America’s salad bowl. It’s a vital source of water to Yuma County, Arizona, which grows 90% of the leafy greens the country consumes in the winter — but it’s nearing a crisis point.
With the river’s water levels at record lows, Arizona is poised to take the biggest cuts: about 30% of its Colorado River supply in 2027 and 2028.

Those are the terms stipulated by the Bureau of Reclamation, which imposed a mandatory two-year plan after the seven states that use Colorado River water failed to reach an agreement. If the megadrought persists and water levels continue to fall, a 10-year management plan the bureau has proposed would allow even harsher cuts that could threaten the country’s winter greens.

“If you cut us off at the knees, or if you restrict the water, it has a national impact,” said Jonathan Lines, a member of the Yuma County Board of Supervisors. “It’s a national security issue and a food security issue.”

Arizona’s agriculture is one rather large ripple of the Colorado River crisis, whose full scale is almost impossible to grasp. About 40 million people in Western states rely on the river for drinking water, but it is shrinking from overuse, drought and climate change. Utilities also depend on it to generate electricity at the dams on Lake Mead and Lake Powell, where much of the water is stored, but both reservoirs hit record lows this month.

title: Four baby goats at mobile petting zoo in North Carolina test positive for rabies
summary: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment.
story: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment.

The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said anyone who had contact with the baby goats at Farm Adventures’ location in Harmony, North Carolina, or at one of its mobile events between July 28 and Thursday should contact local health officials.
“The petting zoo held off-site events involving children and elderly individuals across multiple counties within that time frame,” the department said.
Health professionals may determine whether people who had contact with the baby goats need further examination or precautionary medication, it said.
Without it, rabies is almost always fatal in humans, the state health department said.
Farm Adventures said in a statement posted to Facebook that it is monitoring its other animals for signs of the viral disease.
“The affected animals, our four precious baby goats, have been euthanized to prevent further spread,” it said.
The baby goats were too young for vaccination and were bitten by a skunk that was found in their separate pen, the petting zoo said.
It said it was unaware the goats had been bitten, and that they did not show typical symptoms of the disease. After the first goat’s death, the petting zoo sent its body to be tested, it said.
It was unclear when the skunk was found in the pen.
Skunks are one of the animals most often found with rabies, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

People can get rabies through pets, wild animals and other humans through a bite, a scratch or even infected saliva, it said.  It can take weeks after exposure for early symptoms to begin, including flulike illness, feeling weak, fevers, headaches and a prickling or itching sensation, health officials say.
North Carolina hasn’t had a reported human case since 2011, the state health department said.
Roughly 100,000 Americans a year receive a rabies vaccine following a potential exposure, according to the CDC. It characterizes rabies as “a rare but serious public health concern.”
The petting zoo said it’s cooperating with state and local government officials.

“We are working closely with public health officials, the North Carolina Department of Agriculture, and animal control to address this issue and ensure the safety of our animals and clients,” it said in its statement.
The petting zoo, responding to a comment on Facebook, said it’s hoping its customers are unaffected.
“I am truly concerned about anyone that has been able to enjoy our animals,” the comment said. “We would NEVER intend to put anyone in danger.”
NBC News has reached out to the petting zoo for additional comment.

title: Taylor Swift donates $50,000 to mother who was seriously injured in car accident
summary: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in a car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed.
story: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in a car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed.

Ashley Taunton, a married mother of three, was driving on I-95 in Hopkinton during a torrential rainstorm on July 18 when she saw a car in front of her hydroplane off the road. She pulled over and ran to help the teenagers inside the crashed vehicle, her husband, Joe Taunton, told NBC affiliate WJAR of Providence.
As she was helping them, another vehicle hydroplaned and barreled toward them, he said.
“In a split-second act of pure bravery, Ashley pushed the other person out of harm’s way, taking the brunt of the impact herself,” according to an online fundraiser to support her medical bills.

Joe Taunton said his wife suffered a severe leg injury and extensive internal injuries, including damage to her small and large intestines, liver lacerations and a ruptured diaphragm that caused one of her lungs to collapse. She has undergone at least three surgeries, he said.

Ashley Taunton has documented her recovery on social media, sharing photos of her in a hospital bed in an induced coma, with a nasogastric tube for a small bowel obstruction, staples on her stomach, and — more recently — back home in a leg brace.
On Friday, she posted on Instagram about Swift’s donation, writing: “This is absolutely mind-blowing and so very humbling.”

“@taylorswift you are a beautiful soul I wish I could hug you IRL. Maybe the next time your in Westerly 😘 I live 20 minutes away 🫶 Thank you Jesus for so many amazing humans. This is unbelievable and I am overwhelmed with gratitude. To God be the glory!” she wrote.

title: They were among baseball’s best teams last year. Now they could miss the playoffs.
summary: The Seattle Mariners and the Tampa Bay Rays were World Series contenders last season but are struggling mightily just to reach the postseason.
story: The Toronto Blue Jays were two outs away from winning the World Series last season. Nine months later, they might not even make the playoffs.
“We got to start winning,” Blue Jays manager John Schneider said in July as his team fell under .500. “That’s just the bottom line.”

That regression would seem to have opened an opportunity for the Seattle Mariners, who lost to Toronto in last year’s American League Championship Series ... if the Mariners weren’t similarly having trouble following up their own breakthrough 2025 season.
“Ultimately, we’re just playing very, very, very bad baseball in every facet of the game,” Mariners star Cal Raleigh told reporters this month.

That isn’t how either franchise envisioned this season going when they began the spring with enormous expectations and anticipation for how both might follow up each team’s best season in a generation. Last season, the Jays’ 94 wins tied for the American League’s best record with the New York Yankees, while Seattle had 90 wins. Now, as the teams meet Friday for a three-game series, both are under .500 and on the bubble of grabbing the final wild-card spot with a month to go in the regular season.

Their seasonlong struggles have created a wide-open race for the pennant in the American League. After having won 77 games all last season, the Tampa Bay Rays (79-54) are in first place, with New York (75-57) right behind, even though Yankees star Aaron Judge hasn’t played since he injured a rib in late April. The Boston Red Sox (73-60), despite having fired most of their coaching staff only weeks into the season, have the third-best record. Most surprising of all are the Chicago White Sox, who are 70-63 only two seasons after they won just 41 games. Trying to keep up are seven teams that are within six games of .500 — including Toronto and Seattle.
Each got here in part because of offenses in steep decline. Last season, both ranked in the top five in the American League in runs scored, walks, on-base percentage and slugging percentage.

This season, the Blue Jays have drawn the fewest walks in the AL and have the league’s worst on-base percentage, a category in which the Mariners rank fourth worst. They rank third and fourth worst in slugging percentage. Last year, both teams comfortably outscored their opponents; this year, each has a negative run difference.

Schneider, the Blue Jays’ manager, sensed trouble brewing immediately as the season began. Routine miscues, including in routine actions like tagging up and fielding bunts, sank the team to an inauspicious 4-4 start.
“We’re eight games into the season, and I feel like we’ve had some games that scream ‘not us,’” Schneider told reporters April 4. “And when we play ‘us,’ we’re good.”
But Toronto has rarely been good this season, even though Dylan Cease has become a Cy Young Award candidate as one of the best pitchers in the league, allowing only nine home runs and a .175 average.
By July 20, as the team fell eight games under .500, Schneider said he shared players’ frustration.
“I’m frustrated with them,” he said. “I’m not mad at them.”

The most puzzling element of Toronto’s slide is the lack of power from superstar hitter Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Last fall, his eight home runs in just 18 playoff games pushed the Blue Jays into their first World Series since 1993 and to the brink of a title. By this week, however, Guerrero had homered only seven times in 117 games, including none at home.

“I lose sleep ... and we need to do a better job,” Ross Atkins, Toronto’s executive vice president and general manager, said this month in a radio appearance about Guerrero’s season. “It has been very disappointing that we haven’t been able to provide the right support for him and the right feedback loop that is correcting this challenge right now.”

“To point to exactly what’s happening, listen, yes, we have an understanding of some of the differences. Whether they’re biomechanical, play and approach, there are some subtle differences. There’s no glaring, alarming concern. ... Once those small differences start to become patterns, retraining them while you’re trying to maintain confidence is a very difficult thing.”

A rash of injuries has rarely allowed the Mariners to field the lineup they expected for more than a couple of weeks; in one case, infielder Brendan Donovan sustained a concussion practicing in a batting cage.

Some NFL players are trying to go back to college — if they can find a conference that will let them

But those who are on the field have struggled mightily, as well, with no one more prominent than Cal Raleigh. His 60 home runs last season obliterated the previous single-season catcher home run record of 48 as the “Big Dumper” became a sensation and came within a few votes of winning the AL Most Valuable Player award.
This season, he has hit just 18 home runs as his batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage have all cratered to levels well below his career averages.
Nearly half the balls he hit last season were hit “hard,” by Baseball Reference’s metric. This season, that rate is down to 37%.

“It starts with me; I’m awful. It is what it is,” Raleigh said Aug. 11 after a loss to the Yankees. “I have to find a way to be better and help the guys along. We just have to play better, ultimately.”

Raleigh has begun to find answers, homering in four consecutive at-bats in late August. In a sign of just how jumbled the American League has been this season, the Blue Jays and the Mariners aren’t yet out of the race for the postseason, with both three games behind the final wild-card spot.
The question is whether they can recapture last season’s magic to actually do it.
CORRECTION (Aug. 28, 2026, 11:52 a.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified the second team in the subheadline. It’s the Toronto Blue Jays, not the Tampa Bay Rays.

title: Iran’s supreme leader urges Gulf rulers to confront ‘real enemy’ in written message
summary: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
story: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
The ⁠message was published on Khamenei’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad.
It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who ⁠creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” ​helps ⁠Islam’s enemies.
It asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” if Muslims had been united.

Khamenei has not ⁠been seen in public since being injured in U.S.-Israeli airstrikes six ​months ⁠ago that launched the ‌Iran war, killing his father and previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

His call for unity echoes a statement he made ‌on Friday to Iranians, when he said ‌he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale.

Khamenei specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers ⁠whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.”

Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Gulf Arab monarchies have viewed Iran’s revolutionary ideology, including its anti-monarchic rhetoric and regional influence, as a threat to their ‌political systems.
During the present conflict, Tehran has struck ​U.S. military facilities as well as other infrastructure in ‌Gulf states, underscoring the tensions ⁠between Tehran and its Gulf neighbours.

“My emphatic and repeated recommendation ⁠to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia ‌and the Gulf, is ​to identify your real enemy, ‌understand his plan and confront it,” ​Khamenei said.
War weighs on Iran’s economy

Iranian leaders have acknowledged the economic toll of war with the U.S., with the supreme leader urging the government to ​address the hardship and the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by a third due to the American sanctions and blockade.

Yet Tehran signalled no retreat on Saturday, ‌vowing to withstand U.S. pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it said was control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets.

The government said in a statement on state media that addressing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war was a central focus, including curbing inflation, managing markets, creating jobs, directing investment towards domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.

Six months after the U.S. and ​Israel launched the war, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”.
President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.

Later on Saturday, Pezeshkian called on state TV for a revival of the interim deal, which was signed on June 17 but quickly unravelled amid disagreements over what had been agreed, especially ​on the status of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We ​can solve our problems and gain our ⁠privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said of a document that had offered Iran, among other things, immediate relief from U.S. sanctions and the release of its frozen assets.

title: He Lived 10 Minutes From Where Dolly Parton Grew Up. She Helped Him Attend His Dream School
summary: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.
story: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.

The small mountain town is only 10 miles from Dollywood and about 16 from Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up. Earlier this year, Harper found out he had been chosen as the recipient of the 2026 Dolly Parton Scholarship, making his connection to the iconic late superstar even sweeter.

“Somebody should have told this kid in 12 years he’d be chasing dreams he doesn’t even know he has yet,” he wrote on Instagram in May, alongside a video sharing the news. “Thank you @dollyparton for helping make this kid’s dream come true.”
Parton died at the age 80 on Aug. 25, with fans and friends mourning the country icon, including Harper who posted a musical tribute to his “inspiration.”
In his video, he performs her 1987 song “Wildflowers” and notes that without Parton he “literally wouldn’t be where I am today.”

He recently started as a freshman at Belmont University in Nashville, telling NBC News that the $15,000 he got from the Dolly Parton Scholarship was the last bit he needed to attend his dream school where he’s studying songwriting.

“Dolly’s been a huge thing for me. And when I got in my freshman year (of high school), I fell in love with music completely,” Harper says, sharing he then knew he wanted to be a musician. “... And the best person I could look to was Dolly Parton because she grew up 10 minutes from my house.”

He shares how Parton was “everything” to his community. He says his brother was born at the Dolly Parton Birthing Unit at Covenant Health LeConte in Sevierville, Tennessee, and he attended elementary school “where all of her nieces and nephews went.” He was also part of Parton’s Imagination Library, which sends out free children’s books every month.
“I used to call her the Book Lady because she would always send books,” he says. “That’s just how I knew her as when I was young.”
When he was 14, he played at The Pines Downtown in Sevierville, “where Dolly played her first paid show when she was 10,” he says.
“I remember my mom made a huge deal of that, and it meant nothing to me at the time because I just didn’t understand it,” Harper recalls. “But now that means the world to me.”

This past year, he decided to apply to The Dolly Parton Scholarship, which is part of The Dollywood Foundation. The scholarship provides funds to students who “have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams,” per the website.
Now enrolled in his first year of college and in the songwriting program, Harper is grateful for the opportunities Parton and the scholarship provided him.
“I just hope one day I can be as big an artist as Dolly,” he says. “And I hope that I can also give back to my community and be a good influence on the world.”

title: Justus Kelley Reacts to Being the 1st Miss USA to Be a Married Mom in Her 30s
summary: Justus Kelley made history as Miss USA winner who is a mom, wife and woman in her 30s. Here’s what to know.
story: Justus Kelley just made history as Miss USA 2026. She’s the first married woman, and the first woman in her 30s to win the pageant, Miss USA confirmed to TODAY.com.
The day after the Miss Virginia winner was crowned Miss USA 2026 on Aug. 27, Kelley tells TODAY.com what the moment of being crowned felt like.

“I feel like I left my heart on that stage, and I was so proud of what I had done this week, not just on stage, but each piece of how I decided to show up, bringing a message with me, doing everything with purpose and a mission in mind,” Kelley says.
“That, for me, is what I came to do, and so I really did feel like no matter what happens, I feel like I won. I just felt so much peace. I felt contentment.”
Until recent rule changes in 2023 and 2024, Miss USA prohibited women who were over the age of 28, or who were mothers, pregnant, married or divorced from entering the pageant.
As part of Miss USA’s 75th year celebration, Kelley was joined on stage by legacy queens.
“What we’re doing is only because of the shoulders that we’re standing on, the people that came before us,” Kelley says of meeting the legacy queens.

“I literally had to do my best to contain my excitement all week as I was meeting different former Miss USA’s, just in disbelief that I was meeting them in real life,” Kelley says. “These are women that I follow on social media and have followed throughout the years, and have looked up to them for so much of my life. So to now have these women be people that are welcoming me into a sisterhood just felt like a dream.”

Kelley is a foster parent. She and her husband, Tyler Kelley, are currently foster parents to a sibling set and have fostered previous children. Kelley is also the founder of Foster Footprints, a DMV-based foster support program.
She says she looks at her pageants, and the newest title, as a bigger way to raise awareness about the realities of foster care.
“I went to Miss USA, and I thought, how can I be intentional about my message and my purpose? Just being embedded in everything that I do,” she says.

“I’m very honest and transparent with people about how much I’ve learned since becoming a foster parent,” Kelley adds. “I had a little bit of an ignorance as to what kids would experience. I kind of assumed that every child in this situation must come from an awful situation or an awful parent. And my reality and what I’ve seen from the kiddos that have come into my home is they are coming oftentimes from families that deeply love them but are struggling, have fallen on hard times, are having housing crises and dealing with addiction.”

Kelley’s commitment to shedding light on the realities of the U.S. foster care system is evident in her Miss USA campaign. As she traveled to Miami, where this year’s competition was hosted, she carried trash bags. In an Instagram post, she explained why.

“The trash bags I carry reflect a reality far too many foster children know all too well. A trash bag should never be a child’s suitcase. Every foster child deserves to carry their belongings with dignity — and I need you to help me make that possible,” Kelley wrote in the caption.

The Arlington resident, who holds a master’s degree in public health administration, is also a senior philanthropic adviser for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Arlington, according to her LinkedIn.
With pageant competitions as one of her many hustles, Kelley finds community. She tells TODAY.com what went into her decision to pursue the contests.

“I was a freshman or maybe sophomore in college at the time, just looking for community, looking for like-minded, strong women that wanted to empower and support each other, looking for those types of friendships,” she says. “I found that with pageant women, after doing my first one, I just loved it. I loved the experience and what I got out of it, being in a room full of women that inspire me. That is what keeps me coming back.”

Kelley says her family could not have been more supportive and proud throughout her pageant journey. She says they have been a part of this journey for several years, and that this dream of hers has become their dream.

“My husband keeps calling himself Mr. USA. I don’t know if that’s a thing. Every family member I talk to, they’re like, ‘I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s aunt. I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s sister,’ and I’m like, ‘What? Bro, I can’t believe I’m Miss USA.’ This is just  the coolest thing for all of us.”

title: When Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
summary: Find out everything you need to know about the “Love Island USA” Season 8 reunion, including when it will stream, so you don’t miss any of the drama.
story: It has been over a month since “Love Island USA” fans said goodbye to the Season 8 cast during the grand finale, and now it is time to catch up with the islanders to see if the romances and friendships have continued outside of the villa.

A few weeks ago, the cast, including winners Bryce Dettloff and Trinity Tatum, the “Core 4” and some divisive islanders came together to film a reunion hosted by Ariana Madix and Andy Cohen. Fans have been waiting to see if rumors about spats between contestants and more tension-filled moments are true. Soon, they’ll get their answers.

Ahead of the Season 8 reunion, Peacock released a teaser that showed Melanie Moreno and Sol Dean bickering, Kenzie Annis seemingly addressing a fallout with Melanie and KC Chandler still harboring resentment for the reactions to his Casa Amor behavior.
Plus, viewers will get to hear updates from Bryce and Trinity and the other finalists about everything that has happened since they re-entered the real world.
Find out everything you need to know about the Season 8 reunion so you don’t miss any of the drama.
When Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
The “Love Island USA” Season 8 reunion, led by host Ariana Madix and Bravo’s Andy Cohen, will be released on Monday, Aug. 31.
The reunion was taped in front of a live studio audience and it will feature all the OG islanders and bombshells fans couldn’t stop talking about all season long.
Where to Watch the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion

The streamer recently announced that “Love Island USA” will return for a ninth season next year with Madix as host.
